title: Chapter 73: The Hall of Lots
content:
They read the six names on the ridge at sunrise, with the mist still lying in the valley below the wall.

Wang Meng read them the way he always did, slowly, with each man's village and his mother's name, and after each one the crowd answered. There were four Heaven's Shields, a chain sailor from the Gull Isles who had been seventeen, and one of Zhao Mu's riders who had gone down under a chariot wheel on the river flank. Old Crab answered for the sailor, because the boy's own mother was dead, and his voice did not shake at all.

Ye Wan'er stood between Ye Shuang and Ye Chuan with her hands folded and her pale braid tucked inside her collar. When the last name was read she looked up at Ye Feng, and he saw that she had been counting the graves.

"One hundred and twenty-two," she said quietly, when they walked back down. "Brother, I want every one of their families on the Xingmu purse. Not wages. Something for the children."

"Wang Meng already pays them a pension."

"Then I will pay a second one," she said. "The tree can afford it, and the families can't."

He looked at her for a moment, and then nodded, and she wrote it on her slate as if it had been her idea all along, which it had.

Nangong Kuo's wife and two sons had come through the gate at first light, as kin always did, and stood at the back of the crowd on the ridge in their Zhou robes, listening to names they did not know. Afterwards the old general asked Han Xin for work, not rest, and Han Xin gave him the supply road of the Wangyue Army.

"He opened a king's granaries once," Han Xin told Ye Feng. "He can keep ours full."

He used the rewards in the hall of the Mansion before breakfast, because a card in a pouch did nothing for anyone.

Han Xin and Wang Meng sat with him at the long table, and Ye Xing at the end of it with her bow across her knees. The storage pouch lay open in front of him. He took out the three Talent Summon Cards first and laid them in a row on the wood, three cards of pale grey with a thin line of gold round the edge.

"Two stewards," said Wang Meng, before he could ask. "Men who can hold a territory when I am not there, and grow it. We will have more land than I have hands, my lord, very soon."

"And one man who can hold a wall," said Han Xin. "A place without a wall is a place that belongs to whoever arrives first."

Ye Feng picked up the first card, and thought of a quiet room full of ledgers, and a valley of rice under a big sky. He picked up the second and thought of granaries, long and dry and full. He picked up the third and thought of a gate in the hills, closed, with a lamp burning above it.

The cards grew warm in his hand, one after another, and went to light.

[Talent Summon Cards (A+): 3 used. The answers come with the next dawn.]

Then he took out the folded blueprint, and unfolded it on the table so the others could see. It was drawn on something that was not quite paper, thin and grey and cool to the touch, and on it was a long low building with a drying loft, a steaming shed and a row of benches under a covered walk.

[Epic blueprint: HORN BOW WORKS. Horn, sinew and wood become bows that shoot farther and stronger than any bow of plain wood. For the army only.]

"Beside the forge," said Ye Feng. "Tie Shou will want it where he can shout at it."

"He will want it inside the forge," said Ye Xing. "And he will say the forge is too small."

The blueprint went to light. Out on the flat ground beside Tie Shou's forge, the air shimmered, and the long low building was simply there, with smoke already rising from the steaming shed, as though it had always been part of the town.

[HORN BOW WORKS: built.]

They walked down to see it. Tie Shou was already inside, turning slowly in the middle of the floor with his mouth open. Lira had come up from Bull Valley with a basket of Iron-Horn horn on her back, black and heavy and shining, from the bulls that had died in the defence. She set it down on a bench and stroked one of the horns with two fingers, the way she stroked the calves.

"Nine hundred live bulls," she said, "and every one of them grows a new pair every spring. You will never run short, Master Tie."

Tie Shou did not answer. He had picked up a horn and was bending it very slightly in his big hands, listening to it.

Ye Xing took down the horn bow from her shoulder, the first one, the short black bow Tie Shou had made for Ye Feng before the Summons. She strung it, drew it, and let the string go slowly forward without an arrow.

"With a building like this," she said, "he can make fifty of these in a season. My Daughters of the Sky could shoot over the heads of anyone who stands against us."

"Fifty," said Tie Shou, finding his voice at last. "A hundred, Lady Ye, if the lord leaves me alone and stops sending me bulls."

Ye Feng reached into the storage pouch again and took out a thick book bound in boards of dark wood, with a bronze clasp gone green with age. He put it on the bench beside the horns.

[Manual: BRONZE OF THE SHANG FOUNDRIES. How the founders of the Shang mixed copper and tin, built their clay moulds, and poured bronze that did not crack.]

"From the field at Muye," he said. "The old founders knew things we have forgotten. Arrowheads, buckles, fittings for the bows. And one day, the chariot."

Tie Shou wiped his hands very carefully on his apron before he touched it. He opened it at the first page, a drawing of a mould in three pieces, and did not look up again for some time.

"Master Tie," said Ye Xing, "you have stopped breathing."

"Leave me be," said Tie Shou. "I am reading."

The three hundred jars of field salve he took out next, row by row on the floor of the new works, until two of Maelis's helpers came up with a handcart and wheeled them away to her clinic beside the Xingmu. Maelis kept back thirty of them and sent them back to the Mansion with a note in her small careful hand: For the lord's pouch. He goes where the wounded are.

The gold token was the last thing in the pouch.

Ye Feng put it on the table between Han Xin and Wang Meng. It was the size of his palm, round, heavy, and faintly warm, with the Ledger's crescent cut into one face and nothing at all on the other.

[Territory Token (Gold). Plant it on unclaimed land with water, and a new territory will grow there under your banner.]

"Teja's letter came yesterday," said Wang Meng. He unfolded it. Teja wrote the way she talked, short and plain, in a big round hand. "The road is cut to the valley. The mine is open. The iron is good. There are a hundred and forty families of charcoal burners in the hills around it who belong to nobody, and a river, and two hundred of my diggers who want to stay. Bring the lord. Bring bread."

Han Xin smiled very slightly.

"Then Kunyu it is," said Ye Feng. "Iron for the army, and a second range for Lira's bulls. Who holds it?"

Wang Meng had clearly been waiting for that question. He turned in his chair and said, "Lu Qing," in the voice he used for calling a clerk, and a man came in from the passage where he had evidently been standing for some time.

He was perhaps thirty-five, lean, with ink on two fingers of his right hand and a ring of keys at his belt, and he bowed exactly as deep as a quartermaster ought to bow to his lord and not a hair deeper. Ye Feng had seen him a hundred times on the harbour and in the storehouses, counting sacks with Qiu Ning, standing at the Garrison's door with a tally board while the levies came in. He had never once looked at him with the Eyes.

He looked now.

[Lu Qing. Talent: Quartermaster (B).]

[★★★★ · Path: The Full Storehouse. Where he keeps the stores, nobody goes hungry and nothing goes missing.]

"He has kept the Garrison's stores since the Town rose," said Wang Meng. "In all that time, not one sack has gone missing. Not one arrow. I have checked." He paused. "Twice."

"Three times, Master Wang," said Lu Qing politely. "I saw you on the third."

Ye Feng laughed before he could help it, and Lu Qing looked faintly pleased with himself.

"Then you go to Kunyu," said Ye Feng. "As governor. You'll have Teja for the mine, and a garrison from the Garrison, and whatever else you can talk Master Wang into giving you."

"That will not be much, my lord," said Lu Qing. "But I will make it go a long way."

At noon the Ledger opened its new house, and it did not open it in Wangyue.

Ye Feng was sitting in the long room at the top of the Mansion with Ye Wan'er at his elbow and her abacus on her knee. Han Xin stood at the window. Ye Chuan had come in uninvited and was leaning on the back of his chair, reading the notice over his shoulder for the third time.

[SYSTEM AUCTION · THE FIRST SALE. The Hall of Lots opens at noon. A bidding seat costs a bond of 100 gold, returned when the hall closes. Lords without a bond may watch from the gallery. Each lord may bring one second, who may speak but may not bid.]

"One second," said Ye Chuan at once. "Brother. I can count."

"You can count to the end of a sword," said Ye Wan'er, without looking up. "I'm going."

Han Xin smiled very slightly at the window, and said nothing, which settled it.

Ye Feng put a hundred gold into the bond, and felt Ye Wan'er's hand close on his sleeve, and the long room went white.

When he could see again, he was sitting in a hall that no hand had ever built.

It was round, and very large, and made of dark wood that shone like old lacquer, with tier upon tier of seats rising up from a small stone floor in the middle. The roof was a night sky, deep and clear, with a silver crescent hanging in it that was the crescent of the Ledger. Above every seat a lord's banner hung from a thin gold rod. High round the top of the hall ran a gallery, and the gallery was packed so full of shadowy shapes that it looked like a second roof.

[Lords seated: 611. Lords in the gallery: 3,301.]

Ye Wan'er was sitting beside him in her plain grey dress, with her abacus still on her knee, as if she had carried it in with her. She looked round once, slowly, the way she looked round a market before she bought anything, and then she leaned close to him.

"Brother," she said. "Everyone can see everyone."

He had seen it too. The seats had been given out by lot, and the lot had not cared who anyone was. Over his own head hung the Wangyue banner, the silver crescent on midnight purple, and on his right sat a big, sunburned lord from somewhere in Yangzhou who kept wiping his hands on his knees. Shen Yan was six rows below and to the left, under the white qilin on dark red, with his plain dark armour and his calm, unhurried face. He did not look up. Zhao Lei of Iron Crown sat almost opposite, a heavy man with a red sash and a lot of rings, staring round the hall as though he were working out which of them he could rob.

The Nine Gates were everywhere, and they did not like it. The lot had scattered them over the hall like spilled rice. Ye Feng counted four of their black banners with the nine gold gates on them, each in a different row, and their lords sat stiffly under them in silk, as if the seats were beneath them.

On the stone floor in the middle of the hall stood a tall figure in a grey robe, with a mask of plain silver where its face should have been. It held a small silver hammer. In front of it was a table of black stone, and on the table, nothing at all.

"Lords," said the figure. Its voice came to every seat at once, quiet and close, as though it were standing at each lord's shoulder. "I am the Lotkeeper. Ten lots will be sold today. Each lot has a base price, which is where the bidding starts, and a buyout price. Raise the white tally at your seat and speak your bid. No bid may rise by less than ten gold. If a lord rings the red bell at his seat, he pays the buyout price, and the lot is his at once."

There was a small red bell on the arm of Ye Feng's seat, and a white jade tally beside it. Ye Wan'er looked at the bell the way other girls looked at snakes.

"Lot One is sealed," said the Lotkeeper. "It will be sold last. It has no buyout. We begin with Lot Two."

title: Chapter 74: Spoken For
content:
The first lot lay on the black table before the Lotkeeper had finished speaking, and a panel opened above it for every lord in the hall.

[LOT TWO: THE OFFICER'S WRIT (Rare). Name one common soldier of your army. He rises at once to captain, and the men he leads will follow him as if he had led them for years. Base 100. Buyout 500.]

There was a murmur round the hall at that. Every lord in it had soldiers, and almost none of them had enough men who could lead other men. The tallies went up all over the tiers, and the price ran from a hundred to two hundred while Ye Feng was still reading.

He did not bid. He had the Eyes, and every dawn the Ledger sent him people whose paths he could see. He let it go.

At two hundred and thirty a thin, anxious young lord from Pei, with a Bronze banner and a willow tree sewn on it, stood up in his seat as if the words had been pulled out of him.

"Two hundred and forty!"

Nobody went higher. The young man sat down very fast and stared at his hands.

"Once," said the Lotkeeper. "Twice. Sold."

[Lot Two: Lord HanNing_jr of Willow Bend. 240 gold.]

"He has one good sergeant," said Ye Wan'er softly, "and he's just spent everything he had to make him a captain. I like him."

[LOT THREE: Manual (Epic): THE SWORD BOOK OF THE NANYANG FORGES. How the iron-masters of Wan fold, quench and temper the ring-pommel sabre, so that it bends and does not break. For the army only. Base 200. Buyout 1,000.]

On the black table lay a long, straight, single-edged blade with an iron ring at its pommel, and beside it a book bound in dark boards.

"Brother," said Ye Wan'er. She did not say anything else, and she did not need to. Half the Garrison's new levies were drilling with sticks, and Tie Shou had been complaining for a month that he could make a good spearhead in his sleep and a good sabre almost never.

"Two hundred," said Ye Feng.

It went up fast. A lord from Yan went to four hundred, and a heavy lord in a red sash with a great many rings went to five hundred, and looked round the hall as he said it. Ye Feng knew the banner, an iron crown on grey: Zhao Lei of Iron Crown, whose talent was for gear and forges, and who would want this book more than almost anyone in the room.

"Six hundred," said Ye Feng.

"Six hundred and fifty," said Zhao Lei at once.

Ye Feng glanced at Ye Wan'er. She moved one bead.

"Six hundred and fifty is his," she murmured. "He bid it too fast. He's angry, not rich."

"Seven hundred," said Ye Feng, and saw Zhao Lei's jaw work, and saw him look down at his own hands as if there were a sum written on them, and not lift his tally again.

[Lot Three: Count Ye Feng of Wangyue. 700 gold.]

[LOT FOUR: Blueprint (Rare): SALT TERRACES. Stepped pans cut into a sea cliff. Salt yield three times over. Base 60. Buyout 500.]

"Eighty," said Ye Feng.

A lady lord in crimson silk in the second row turned in her seat to look up at him. She had a sharp, handsome face and a crimson peony on her banner, and she raised her own tally without taking her eyes off him.

"A hundred."

"She sells salt up the Kuaiji coast," Ye Wan'er murmured. "If she has terraces, her salt is cheaper than ours. If we have them, ours is cheaper than hers."

They went up together in tens. At a hundred and seventy the lady in crimson stopped, and looked at him for a long moment, and then turned her back on him.

[Lot Four: Count Ye Feng of Wangyue. 180 gold.]

"Mak Senah will cry," said Ye Wan'er, writing it on her slate. "Then she will make you build it on the Gull Isles, where the cliffs are."

[LOT FIVE: Charter (Epic): THE IRON-CLAD RIDERS. Choose a hundred trained soldiers. By the next dawn they are heavy cavalry, man and horse in iron, with lances and the skill to use them. Base 300. Buyout 1,500.]

Before anyone could raise a tally, a line opened in the corner of Ye Feng's sight. From the way the whole hall went still, it had opened in front of every lord at once.

[Whisper · Ouyang Mingde of the Nine Gates: Lot Five is spoken for. So is Lot Seven. The Nine Gates remember their friends. They also remember the others.]

Ye Feng found him a moment later, four rows down, a plump, soft-handed man in brown silk with a jade ring on every finger, sitting with his hands folded on his belly like a merchant who has already sold the shop. The Divine Eyes opened before he asked them to.

[Ouyang Mingde. The Nine Gates. Talent: Counting House (A).]

"Three hundred," said Gongsun Hao of the Nine Gates, from the far side of the hall, and lowered his tally, and waited.

Nobody moved.

Six hundred lords sat with their hands in their laps, looking at a charter that would have turned a hundred of their best men into iron-clad riders, for a fifth of what it was worth. Ye Feng saw the big sunburned lord beside him look at his own tally, and then at the floor.

"So that's how they do it," said Ye Wan'er, very quietly. "They don't outbid anyone. They just tell everyone not to bid."

Ye Feng was looking at the little picture on the black table: a rider and his horse in iron from brow to hoof, a long lance couched under his arm. He thought of the Wind Riders, quick and light on the river flank at Muye, and of what a hundred men like that would do to a shield wall.

"Can we?" he said.

Ye Wan'er's fingers flew over the beads, and stopped.

"We can," she said. "Brother, it's worth fifteen hundred to any army in this hall, and they mean to have it for three. Make them pay for it, or take it."

"Once," said the Lotkeeper. "Twice."

Ye Feng raised his tally.

"Four hundred."

The hall went so quiet that he could hear the little monk at the back sniffing. Gongsun Hao's head turned slowly. So did Ouyang Mingde's.

"Five hundred," said Gongsun Hao.

"Six hundred."

"Seven hundred," said Gongsun Hao, and looked across the hall at Ouyang Mingde, and Ye Feng understood that the man with the rings had not expected to need more than the base, and had not given his lords the gold to fight with, because he had never needed to.

"Eight hundred," said Ye Feng.

Gongsun Hao's tally rose an inch, and stayed there, and he looked at Ouyang Mingde again. Ouyang Mingde was looking at his rings.

"Nine hundred," said Ye Feng.

Gongsun Hao put his tally down on the arm of his seat, very gently, the way a man puts down a cup he wants to throw.

"Once. Twice. Sold."

[Lot Five: Count Ye Feng of Wangyue. 900 gold.]

The gallery broke into noise. A line opened in the corner of Ye Feng's sight.

[Whisper · Ouyang Mingde: The lord of Wangyue is new to these things. He does not know how they are done.]

Ye Feng did not answer it.

"You've made an enemy," said Ye Wan'er.

"I had one already," said Ye Feng. "Now he knows my face."

[LOT SIX: Scroll (Rare): THE LANTERN OF WORTHY MEN. Hang it over your gate, and wandering men and women of talent will find their way to your land a little more often. Base 100. Buyout 500.]

Zhao Lei bid for it at once, and bid hard, as if to make up for the sword book, and the smaller lords fell away round him one by one. At two hundred and sixty there was only one other tally still up, at the very back of the hall, under a little brown banner with a lotus on it. It belonged to a small round lord with a shaved head, who was holding it with both hands.

"Two hundred and seventy," said the little lord. "That is all I have."

Zhao Lei smiled round the hall.

"Two hundred and eighty."

Then three small lines flashed across the hall, one after another, for every lord to see.

[Gift: 20 gold from Lord ShenMin_cn to Lord LittleMonk.]

[Gift: 15 gold from Lord LinFang_zz to Lord LittleMonk.]

[Gift: 10 gold from Lord HanNing_jr to Lord LittleMonk.]

The anxious young lord from Willow Bend, who had nothing left at all, had given away ten gold of it. He sat with his arms folded, very red.

The little monk at the back looked at the gifts for a moment as if he could not read them. Then he stood up and said, "Three hundred!" in a voice that cracked in the middle.

Zhao Lei stared at him. He could have gone higher, and everyone in the hall knew it, and everyone in the hall was watching to see whether he would beat a little monk who had just been handed his bid by three strangers. He did not. He sat back with his arms folded, and his face went the colour of his sash.

[Lot Six: Lord LittleMonk of Lotus Ford. 300 gold.]

The gallery cheered. Three thousand people cheered at once, and the Lotkeeper waited for it to finish without moving its silver face.

[LOT SEVEN: Blueprint (Epic): THE BLACK SCALE ARMOUR OF THE WESTERN MARCHES. Heavy armour for horse and rider, iron scales sewn on hide. For the army only. Base 300. Buyout 1,500.]

"Three hundred," said Gongsun Hao, and lowered his tally.

"Three hundred and fifty."

It was a woman's voice, clear and cool, from the front of the hall, and she had plainly been watching Lot Five. She sat under a vermilion banner with a red bird on it, in a plain fighting coat with her sleeves tied back, and she held her tally up as straight as a spear. The gallery made a sound like wind in grass.

"Su Qingluan," said the big lord beside Ye Feng, under his breath. "The Vermilion Bird club. They don't take orders from anyone."

Ouyang Mingde turned his head and looked at her for a long, mild moment. She did not look back at him.

"Five hundred," said Gongsun Hao.

"Six hundred."

"A thousand," said Gongsun Hao, and smiled.

The hall gasped. Su Qingluan's tally stayed up, but Ye Feng saw her other hand close on the arm of her seat. She was adding, the way Ye Wan'er added. Then, slowly, she spoke.

"Twelve hundred."

"Thirteen hundred," said Gongsun Hao, without a pause. "I will ring the bell, lady, if I must. Can you?"

She could not. Ye Feng could see it in the set of her shoulders. Twelve hundred was everything her club had brought into the hall, and the bell was fifteen hundred, and Gongsun Hao had just told the whole hall that he would pay it rather than lose to a woman who would not do as she was told.

Ye Feng looked at Ye Wan'er.

She was already looking at him. She did not smile. She looked down at her beads, and moved three of them from one side to the other, and nodded once.

[Gift: 300 gold from Count Ye Feng of Wangyue to Lord Su Qingluan of Vermilion Hall.]

The line flashed across the hall for every lord to see, and the hall went so quiet that Ye Feng could hear the little monk at the back sniffing.

Su Qingluan read it. She turned in her seat, and found the purple banner, and looked at Ye Feng for one long moment. Then she reached out and rang the red bell at her seat, once, hard, so that the sound went all the way up into the painted sky.

[Lot Seven: Lord Su Qingluan of Vermilion Hall. 1,500 gold. Buyout.]

The gallery came apart. Down on the far side of the hall Gongsun Hao sat with his tally still half raised, as though he had forgotten it was in his hand, and Ouyang Mingde slowly unfolded his hands from his belly for the first time all day.

Ye Wan'er let out a long breath beside him.

"Two lots," she said. "Two lots they said were spoken for, and the whole hall saw what happened to them." She glanced down at the vermilion banner. "And now she knows your face too, Brother."

title: Chapter 75: Lot One
content:
After that the hall was not the same. Lords who had sat on their hands at the first whisper were sitting forward now, and when Lot Eight was called, nobody looked at the black banners first.

[LOT EIGHT: Talisman (Rare): THE SPRING RAIN CHARM. Burn it over your fields, and twenty thousand mu of thin, tired land will wake as rich black soil. Base 100. Buyout 500.]

Ye Feng let it go. Wangyue's fields were young and fat, and the Eldari had their own ways with soil. Aisyah of Langya, under her red and gold banner, took it for two hundred gold after a short fight with three farming lords from the river country, and found his seat with her eyes and touched two fingers to her brow.

[Alliance channel · Aisyah: Thank you for not bidding against me. Grandmother Sun says the Langya fields are lazy.]

[LOT NINE: Blueprint (Epic): THE ARMOUR OF THE UNMOVING WALL. Heavy plate for foot soldiers, iron lamellar from neck to knee. Men who wear it hold a line that horses break against. For the army only. Base 400. Buyout 2,000.]

This time Ye Wan'er did not wait for him to look at her.

"That one," she said. "That's the Heaven's Shields. That's every front rank we will ever have."

"Four hundred," said Ye Feng.

He had a rival at once. It was a lean, weathered lord high on the left, under a grey banner with a running wolf on it, who bid the way a man rides, leaning forward. NorthWolf of Frost Ridge, whom Ye Feng knew only from the rankings and the world chat. They went up together in fifties, with no pause on either side, and the smaller lords fell away round them, until the price stood at nine hundred and fifty and it was NorthWolf's.

"A thousand," said Ye Feng.

NorthWolf leaned back. For a moment he looked across the hall at the purple banner, as one rider looks at another across a field. Then he lifted one hand from his tally, open, and let it fall.

[Lot Nine: Count Ye Feng of Wangyue. 1,000 gold.]

"That's the strong room nearly empty," said Ye Wan'er. She did not sound sorry at all.

[LOT TEN: Manual (Epic): THE BOWYER'S CANON OF THE NORTHERN FRONTIER. Every bow and every crossbow the old frontier armies made, and how to make them. Base 500. Buyout 3,000.]

Ye Feng did not bid. He had the Horn Bow Works standing beside his forge, and Ye Xing, who would not have thanked him for a book that told her how to string a bow. Zhao Lei bid, and bid hard, and was beaten, for the third time that day, by a calm voice from six rows below the purple banner.

"Nineteen hundred," said Shen Yan.

[Lot Ten: Count Shen Yan of Qilin Tower. 1,900 gold.]

"He's been saving," said Ye Wan'er, watching him. "He has bought one thing all day, and he bought the most expensive thing in the hall. Brother, he will be dangerous at the sealed lot."

"Lot One," said the Lotkeeper.

The black table cleared. The gold line round the top of the hall brightened until it hurt to look at, and the seal broke.

[LOT ONE: THE FREE PORT SEAL (Epic). A harbour under this seal becomes a free port. Ships of every lord may trade at its quay. Quay fees and market fees go to the lord of the port. Merchants will come from very far away. Base 200. No buyout.]

Ye Feng felt Ye Wan'er go perfectly still beside him.

"Brother," she said, very softly. "That one."

"I know."

"No, you don't."

Her grey eyes had gone bright and hard, the way they did when she looked at a price.

"Every ship on the coast pays at our quay. Every merchant who comes to buy Wangyue cheese or Wangyue salt stays the night, eats at Kahu's and pays a fee for his stall. It pays every year, forever, and nobody can take it from us without taking the harbour." She took a breath. "Twelve hundred would be fair. But we have eight hundred and seventy left in the strong room, so eight hundred. Not one coin more."

A line opened in the corner of his sight before the first bid.

[Whisper · Ouyang Mingde: The Nine Gates will not bid on Lot One. In return, the lord of Wangyue will not bid against the Nine Gates again. A small thing, between friends.]

Ye Feng closed it.

The bids opened at two hundred and went up in fifties, and this time the tallies that rose were the coast's. A lord from Xu bid, and a lord from Donglai, and the lady in crimson from Kuaiji, who sold salt up the southern coast and had already lost one lot to him today. Aisyah of Langya bid once, at three hundred, and then lowered her tally, and a small line came into the corner of his sight.

[Alliance channel · Aisyah: It should be yours. Your harbour is better than mine. Don't tell Grandmother Sun I said so.]

At four hundred and fifty the lord from Donglai sat back. Then, six rows below, a white tally rose under the white qilin.

"Five hundred," said Shen Yan.

The hall turned to look at him. Ye Feng felt Ye Wan'er lean in close.

"He has no coast," she said softly. "Not a mile of it. He doesn't want a harbour, Brother. He wants to see how deep our purse is."

"Then let's not show him."

Ye Feng did not bid. The lady in crimson went to five hundred and fifty, and looked down at Shen Yan with open dislike. Shen Yan went to six hundred, quite calmly. Then he put his tally down on the arm of his seat, and folded his hands, and did not lift it again.

"Six hundred and fifty," said Ye Feng.

"Six hundred and eighty," said the lady in crimson, at once.

"Seven hundred."

She looked up at the purple banner for a long moment. She was adding something in her head, Ye Feng thought, and the sum was not only gold. Then she laid her tally down on the arm of her seat.

"Keep it, then, lord of Wangyue," she said, clearly enough for the whole hall to hear. "Your harbour is nearer the sea roads than mine. But I will be watching your quay."

"Once," said the Lotkeeper. "Twice. Sold."

[LOT ONE: Count Ye Feng of Wangyue. 700 gold.]

[The Free Port Seal is yours. Set it on a harbour, and the harbour will open.]

[THE HALL OF LOTS is closing. Bonds returned.]

As the hall began to fade, Shen Yan looked up for the first time, straight at the purple banner, across six rows and six hundred lords. His face showed nothing at all. Then the dark wood went white.

Ye Feng opened his eyes in the long room of the Mansion. The light had hardly moved on the floor. Ye Wan'er sat up beside him with a little gasp and grabbed for her abacus, which had slid off her knee, and Ye Chuan, who had evidently been standing behind the chair the whole time, grabbed both of them by the shoulders.

"Well?" he said. "Well? You both went still as stones for an hour and Brother Han wouldn't let me shake you."

"The port," said Ye Wan'er. "For seven hundred. And the salt terraces, and the sword book, and a hundred iron-clad riders that Gongsun Hao said were his, and the armour of the Unmoving Wall. And three hundred gold to a lady who rang a bell in the Nine Gates' faces." She looked at Ye Feng. "Nearly four thousand gold, Brother, and the strong room is almost bare. The salt and the Mi House trade will fill it again. They always do."

Ye Chuan whooped once, very loudly, and then put both hands over his mouth when Han Xin looked at him.

A moment later a small plain line opened in the corner of Ye Feng's sight, with no border at all.

[Private message · QilinTower: Next time, I will not stop.]

Ye Feng read it twice. Then he closed it, and did not answer.

The second message came while Ye Chuan was still asking questions, and it had a small red bird at the start of it.

[Private message · SuQingluan: Vermilion Hall does not take gifts, Count. It takes loans. Three hundred gold, and we will pay it back, with something better than gold. And if the Nine Gates come for you over this, send word south.]

Ye Feng read that one twice as well. Then he wrote back.

[Private message · to SuQingluan: Keep the gold. Send word if they come for you.]

The sword book and the armour went to Tie Shou before supper. Ye Feng laid them out on the bench of the new Horn Bow Works, beside the Iron-Horn horn and the Shang founders' book, and the old smith looked from one to the other for a long time without saying anything at all.

[Epic manual: THE SWORD BOOK OF THE NANYANG FORGES. Learned by the Wangyue forge.]

[Epic blueprint: THE ARMOUR OF THE UNMOVING WALL. Learned by the Wangyue forge.]

"Sabres first," said Tie Shou at last, slowly, with his thick finger on the page about quenching. "The Garrison's new men are drilling with sticks. I can give them iron in a month, and good iron in two." He turned to the armour, and his face changed. "And this. Every scale riveted, neck to knee. My lord, a man in this does not step back."

"The Heaven's Shields first," said Ye Feng. "A hundred sets. Then the front rank of the Wangyue Army."

Tie Shou was already rolling up his sleeves.

"Then go away, my lord," he said, "and send me charcoal."

The charter he gave to Ye Chuan in the Wind Riders' lines, and Ye Chuan, who had been sulking since the noon bell, stopped sulking at once and spent the evening walking up and down his riders with his hands behind his back, choosing.

[Epic charter: THE IRON-CLAD RIDERS. A hundred Wind Riders named. They wake as heavy cavalry at the next dawn.]

They set the seal on the Harbour that evening, at the top of the stone steps, where the two arms of the harbour met the town.

It went into the stone like water into sand, and where it had been there was a round mark in the step, a crescent inside a ring, and the words FREE PORT cut round the edge in letters that every traveller would be able to read, whatever tongue he spoke.

[WANGYUE HARBOUR: FREE PORT. Quay fees: yours. Market fees: yours. The news will travel along every coast.]

Mi Zhu stood looking down at the mark for a very long time with his hands behind his back. Then he looked up at Ye Feng, and his round face was wet.

"My lord," he said. "My grandfather dreamed of a port like this. He used to say that if he ever found one, he would never leave it."

"Then don't," said Ye Feng.

Ye Wan'er had already crouched beside the mark with her slate on her knee, writing down the fees she meant to charge, and Mi Zhu, after a moment, crouched down beside her and began, very gently, to argue.

That evening, at the low tide, Ye Feng took the Family Army through the black door, and they came back with the dawn.

[TOWER RECORD · STAGE 4 · THE RED DUNES · one month inside, one night outside]

[Five Well Lords at war over the water of a dead king's desert. Ye Xing would not fight their riders, only their wells, and one by one their horses went thirsty and they knelt. The glassmakers opened the last city's gate through their own drain.]

[Battles: 5. Fallen: 22. Wounded: 47.]

[Joined: about 4,000 followers with their families; some 200 former desert riders ask to try the monthly trial.]

[Rewards: silver 60,000, armour 1,200 sets, desert horses 200, Merit +1,200. Tribute: 4,000 silver and a crate of glass every payday.]

[Kingdom special: GLASS. The old king's furnace secret comes with its makers.]

[Notable talent: Old Harun, glassmaker of nine generations. Talent: Clear Fire (B).]

[Talent group: the Sand Hawks, a family of twelve desert horse archers. Talent: B+.]

[Ye Family Army battle grade: TRAINED.]

Ye Wan'er was waiting on the rocks with a lantern. She took the first glass cup out of Old Harun's hands, held it up to the light, and did not give it back.

title: Chapter 76: The Answers
content:
Before the sun was up, a hundred riders walked their horses out of the Wind Riders' lines and down to the beach, and the whole camp came out to stare at them. Yesterday they had been light horsemen in leather. This morning they sat their horses in black iron from brow to boot, and their horses wore iron too, from the ears to the knees, and each man carried a long lance that he held as if he had carried it all his life. Ye Chuan rode at their head with his own helmet under his arm, grinning so widely that it looked painful.

[THE IRON-CLAD RIDERS: 100 Wind Riders are now heavy cavalry.]

"Brother," he called up to the shelf, "they can't get on their horses without a mounting block, and they can't get off without falling. They're perfect."

The dawn arrivals came out of the mist at the roots of the Xingmu as they did every morning, twelve hundred of them, blinking at the silver leaves and the town spread out below them.

Ye Feng stood with Wang Meng at the top of the steps cut into the shelf, where the clerks sat with their tally boards and the Commons runners waited to lead the new people down. He had stood here most mornings since the Town rose. He liked to look at their faces. Some were frightened and some were curious, and a few, always a few, looked out over the valley and the harbour and the long wall on the ridge as though they had come home.

Two of them did not look at the town at all. They looked straight up the steps at him.

The first was a tall man of about fifty with a long grey face and a short grey beard, dressed in the plain dark robe of a steward of some great house, with a leather case of papers under his arm. He climbed the steps without hurrying and stopped two steps below Ye Feng, and bowed, and his bow was so exactly right that Wang Meng, beside him, made a small sound of approval.

[Pei Lin. Talent: Steward (A).]

[★★★★ · Path: The Steady Hand. A land he keeps grows a little richer every year, and never all at once.]

"My lord," said Pei Lin. "I kept the lands of the Yang family in the hills below Taishan for twenty-two years. Then the Yellow Turbans came down from the mountain, and the Yang family ran to Luoyang, and the lands are gone." He paused. "I would like to keep some more lands, if my lord has any."

"Master Wang has more than he can carry," said Ye Feng. "He's been asking me for help."

"I have not been asking," said Wang Meng. "I have been mentioning it."

The second was a woman, Malay, perhaps forty, small and square, with a sarong of faded green and a man's jacket rolled to the elbows. She had a bunch of wooden tally sticks tied at her belt that clacked when she walked, and she was humming under her breath as she came up the steps, very quietly, a counting song of the kind women sing in the rice fields.

[Suria. Talent: Granary Keeper (A).]

[★★★★ · Path: The Long Store. In her granaries the grain keeps for seven years, and the rats go hungry.]

She stopped in front of him and did not bow at all. She looked past him at the long granaries on the shelf behind the Commons, and her nose wrinkled very slightly.

"My lord," she said. "Your granaries face the sea."

"They do."

"The wind off the sea is wet. In the autumn rains your grain will sweat, and in the spring you will find a quarter of it gone to mould." She looked at him then, quite kindly. "I can fix that. I will need some men with shovels, and some charcoal, and nobody telling me how to do it."

Wang Meng had a peculiar expression on his face, the expression of a man who has been saying something for a month and has just heard it said by someone else.

"Master Wang," said Ye Feng. "They're yours. Teach them everything."

"With pleasure, my lord."

There should have been a third. Ye Feng looked over the heads of the last arrivals, down the steps, along the path to the Commons, and saw no one else who looked at him the way the first two had.

It was Wang Meng's clerk who found the answer, an hour later, in the reports from the Kunyu road. The road patrol had passed a big man walking inland at dawn, alone, with a pack on his back and a staff in his hand, and when they asked where he was going, he had pointed at the hills and said, There is no wall there yet.

"The card knew where you wanted him," said Wang Meng, folding the report. "Before you did."

There was one more thing in Ye Feng's coat that he had not used yet. He took it up to the watch platform at the top of the Mansion after breakfast, with Mak Senah puffing up the stairs behind him in her wide straw hat.

[Rare blueprint: SALT TERRACES. Stepped pans cut into a sea cliff. Seawater climbs, the sun takes the water, the salt stays. Triples the salt a shore can make.]

From the watch platform the Gull Isles were a low dark line on the sea to the north, with the big island's white cliff catching the morning sun. He opened the Territory Page, found the big island, and touched the cliff.

[Build SALT TERRACES on the Gull Isles: yes.]

The blueprint went to light in his hand. Across the water, so far away that he would not have seen it without the Eyes, the white cliff changed shape. Where it had been a smooth wall there were now steps, long shallow steps going down in rows to the sea, each one shining with a thin skin of water.

Mak Senah stood with both hands holding the brim of her hat and said nothing at all for a long time. Then she sat down very suddenly on the bench by the rail.

"My lord," she said at last, in a small voice. "That is three times the salt. Three times."

"Koa will need people to work them."

"Koa will have them." She was already counting on her fingers. "My two nieces. The Wen girls from the drying racks. Ah Hai's cousins, who are bored." She stood up again. "I will go over on the noon boat."

"You don't have to go today."

"Yes, my lord," said Mak Senah, "I do," and went down the stairs much faster than she had come up.

Mi Zhu and Ye Wan'er had spent the morning in the Harbour office with the door shut, and by the time Ye Feng came down to the quay the fees were painted on a board beside the free port mark, in large clear characters that any captain could read.

He read it twice. It seemed very reasonable, which surprised him.

"A low fee for every ship," said Ye Wan'er, coming out of the office with her abacus under her arm and ink on her chin. "So that every ship comes. A higher fee for a stall in the market, because a merchant who sells here makes money. And nothing at all for a fishing boat from the villages, because they are poor, and because Brother would be cross."

"Who wanted it low?"

"I did," said Mi Zhu, following her out. He looked tired and pleased. "Lady Ye wanted it lower. She says that if the fee is low enough, ships that never meant to stop here will stop just because it's cheaper than not stopping." He shook his head slowly. "She is right. I have been a merchant for thirty years, my lord, and I would not have thought of it until I was fifty."

"You would have thought of it at forty-five," said Ye Wan'er generously.

Mi Zhu laughed. Then he turned to Ye Feng, and his face became serious.

"My lord, with a free port, Wangyue needs a proper trading house. Not only my family's house on the quay. A house for all of Wangyue, with its own name, that buys and sells for the town, so that the salt and the cheese and the fish all go out under one flag." He paused. "I would like your leave to found it."

"Wangyue Commerce," said Ye Feng. "Under Master Wang. Write it up, and we'll found it properly when I'm back from Kunyu."

"You are going to Kunyu?"

"Tomorrow."

Mi Zhu's eyes went to the bread ovens behind the Commons, which had been running since before dawn, and then to the long line of carts on the valley road, loaded with sacks, and he nodded slowly.

"Teja asked for bread," he said. "I see."

They left at first light, a long column winding up the valley road and over the ridge to the west.

There were a thousand men of the Wangyue Garrison, chosen by Wang Meng, with their spears on their shoulders and their packs on their backs, marching four abreast. There were forty carts of bread, rice and tools, and a hundred Wind Riders in front and behind, with Ye Chuan at their head. Lu Qing rode beside the carts with his ring of keys and his tally board, already checking the loads.

And there were the bulls.

Lira had chosen four hundred and fifty of the Iron-Horns to go to the Kunyu hills, where the grass was long and nobody had ever grazed it, and she and Hu Ba were driving them at the back of the column with twenty herders. The bulls did not want to go. They went sideways, and backwards, and into the ditches, and one of them lay down in the road and refused to get up until Lira went and sat on its neck and talked to it.

Ye Chuan rode back to watch, laughing so hard that he almost fell off his horse.

"Brother!" he called. "Brother, the Wind Riders can herd them! We herded cattle every autumn in Pingyuan, before we were outlaws! Give me twenty riders and I'll have them at Kunyu by noon!"

"You stole cattle every autumn in Pingyuan," said Mo Lin, riding beside him.

"From corrupt officials. It's the same skill."

Lira looked up at him from the neck of the bull she was sitting on.

"Lord Ye Chuan," she said. "If you or your riders chase my bulls, I will tell Lady Ye Shuang that you were the one who put the frog in her boot."

Ye Chuan's face went very still.

"How do you know about the frog?"

"Everyone knows about the frog," said Mo Lin.

Ye Chuan rode back to the front of the column without another word, and Ye Feng, beside Ye Xing on the dark green horse, did not laugh, because he was the lord. But it was close.

Teja's road was better than he had expected. It ran up through the hills behind the coast in long easy curves, cut wide enough for two carts to pass, with drains on the uphill side and young trees planted where the slopes were steep. Zhou Ping's woodcutters had made it. At every stream there was a ford paved with flat stones, and at the steepest place a little bridge, and on the bridge someone had carved a crescent moon and the words Teja's road. Don't spit.

Ye Xing laughed out loud when she saw it, a rare clear sound that made the riders nearby turn and smile.

By the middle of the afternoon the hills had grown higher and darker, and the trees had changed from pines to oaks and chestnuts, and there was smoke in the air, thin and blue and sweet. Charcoal smoke. They passed a burner's clearing with its turf mound smoking quietly in the middle, and a family of thin brown people who stood at the edge of the trees and watched them pass without a word.

"A hundred and forty families," said Ye Xing quietly. "Teja said they belong to nobody."

"They look like they belong to somebody," said Ye Feng. "Somebody who doesn't feed them."

They camped that night in a long meadow beside a river, and while the riders saw to the bulls, Ye Feng opened the world chat. The Summons was still all anyone talked about.

[World] Langya: The Duke of Shao has come home with us. He watched the bridge. He says he will judge our cases under a tree, as he did in Zhou.

[World] IronCrown: Fei Lian rides for Iron Crown.

[World] IronCrown: E Lai's father. Ask Wangyue.

Ye Feng closed the panel, and sat for a while looking at the fire.

"He did not fight at Muye," said Ye Xing quietly, when Ye Feng told her. "He was in the north, on the king's errand, when his son died. A father who was not there tends to remember the man who was."

The camp lay a day's march short of the valley, with the bulls lowing in the dark at the edge of the firelight and the Garrison's watch fires in a ring.

It was Mo Lin who came to his fire after midnight, out of the trees, so quietly that Ye Feng did not hear him until he was standing there.

"Brother," he said. "There are fires on the ridge above Teja's valley. Not charcoal fires. Cook fires, a lot of them, and men around them with spears." He squatted down beside the coals. "Four hundred. Maybe five. They've been watching Teja's diggers for days."

title: Chapter 77: No Wall Yet
content:
Teja's valley opened in front of them in the middle of the morning, and Ye Feng understood at once why she had written Bring the lord.

It was a long green bowl in the hills, perhaps two li from end to end, with a quick bright river running down the middle of it and oak woods climbing the slopes on either side. At the head of the valley a dark seam of rock showed through the turf like a bruise, and below it was a black hole in the hillside with a timber frame round its mouth and a heap of red-brown stone beside it. Smoke went up from a dozen turf huts by the river. Somewhere a hammer was ringing on iron.

Teja came down the valley to meet them on a mule, in her faded sarong and her man's jacket, with her cloth bag over her shoulder.

"My lord," she said. "You brought the bread."

"Forty carts."

"Good. My diggers have been living on chestnuts for a week."

She looked past him at the long column of spearmen, and the carts, and the bulls spreading out across the lower meadow with Lira running after them.

"And soldiers. That's even better. Did Mo Lin tell you about the ridge?"

"He told me."

Teja turned on her mule and looked up at the eastern ridge, where the oaks were thick and dark. There was no smoke there now.

"They came at the turn of the moon," she said. "They sit up there and watch us dig. Yesterday two of them came down and told my headman that the charcoal in these hills belongs to the Black Charcoal, and so does anything dug out of the ground with the help of charcoal, and that we should pay them half the iron or go home."

She spat neatly over the mule's shoulder.

"I told them to come down and take it."

"Did they?"

"Not yet."

She looked back at him, and her weather-lined face cracked into a grin.

"But I think they will tonight, now that there are forty carts of bread in the valley."

There was a man sitting on a rock at the mouth of the valley.

Ye Feng had seen him from a long way off, because he was very big and he was not moving. He sat with a staff across his knees and a pack at his feet, looking at the slope in front of him. All along that slope, from the river to the foot of the western ridge, someone had driven a line of wooden stakes into the turf and strung them with a cord, so that a long straight line ran across the mouth of the valley like a mark on a map.

When Ye Feng rode up, the man stood. He was taller than Ye Tian, though not as broad, with a heavy plain face and big quiet hands, and he looked at Ye Feng for a long moment without bowing. Then he bowed, once, very deep.

[Ji Shan. Talent: Fort Warden (A).]

[★★★★ · Path: The Closed Gate. A wall he builds is never taken by the front.]

"My lord," said Ji Shan. His voice was slow and deep. "I am sorry I did not come to the tree. I woke on the road, and the road was going here, and there was no wall here."

He pointed at the line of stakes.

"The wall goes there. Stone below, earth above, a gate by the river. Two months, if I have the men."

"You have a thousand."

Ji Shan looked over Ye Feng's shoulder at the Garrison, marching down into the valley four abreast, and something in his heavy face eased.

"Then six weeks," he said.

"And tonight?"

Ji Shan turned and looked up at the eastern ridge, the way Teja had.

"Tonight," he said, "we use the carts."

They planted the token at noon, on a low green knoll at the bend of the river, where the water ran deep and slow under the bank and the whole valley could be seen from end to end.

Lu Qing stood on one side of him with his tally board, and Teja on the other with her headman, a thin old Han digger called Grandfather Shi who had lost three fingers in some other mine long ago. Ye Xing stood a little behind with her bow. The diggers had come up from the river and the huts, two hundred of them, Yellow Turban joiners who had cut the road and stayed, still with the marks of their headcloths pale on their foreheads. They stood in a half ring around the knoll and watched.

Ye Feng knelt and pressed the gold token into the turf with the heel of his hand.

It went down as if the ground had been waiting for it. For a moment there was nothing. Then the grass on the knoll shivered, all at once, as if a wind had passed over it, and a thin line of silver light ran out from the place where the token had gone, down the knoll, across the meadow, along the river and up both slopes, until it had drawn a ring around the whole valley.

[TERRITORY FOUNDED: KUNYU. Tier: Hamlet. Under the banner of Wangyue.]

[Gold token: 60 arrivals with every dawn. The land will grow as its people grow.]

[Governor: Lu Qing. Garrison: 1,000 of the Wangyue Garrison.]

[Kunyu Iron Seam: good ore. Iron for the army of Wangyue.]

The diggers did not cheer. They looked at the silver ring in the grass, and at each other, and then the oldest of them, Grandfather Shi, went down on his knees on the turf, slowly, because his knees were bad. One by one, and then all together, the others knelt behind him.

"We were going to stay anyway, my lord," said Grandfather Shi, from the ground. "But it is good to stay somewhere that has a name."

Ye Feng helped him up himself.

"It's yours as much as mine," he said. "You cut the road."

Lu Qing had already sat down on the knoll with his tally board on his knee and begun to write. When Ye Feng looked over his shoulder he saw a list headed KUNYU STORES, and under it, in small neat columns: bread 40 carts, rice 600 sacks, picks 200, chestnuts uncounted.

The Black Charcoal came an hour after moonrise, as Teja had said they would.

By then the valley mouth had changed. Ji Shan had spent the afternoon walking up and down his line of stakes with the Garrison's officers, and when the sun went down the forty carts stood along that line, end to end, tipped on their sides with their wheels chained together and their beds facing out. Behind them, in the dark, eight hundred spearmen of the Garrison knelt in two ranks. The bread was in the huts by the river. The watch fires had been built well forward, beyond the carts, so that anyone who came at the line would come through the light, and anyone behind it would be in the dark.

The other two hundred spearmen, and Ye Chuan's hundred riders, were not at the line at all. They were in the oak woods on the lower slope of the western ridge, with Mo Lin.

Ye Feng stood behind the middle of the cart wall with Ji Shan and Ye Xing, Moonripple in his hand.

"They will come straight down the meadow," said Ji Shan. "They think it is a camp. They will see the carts and the fires and think we are asleep."

"And if they come round the side?"

"There is no side."

Ji Shan pointed with his staff, first at the river on the left, deep and fast, and then at the western ridge on the right, steep and thick with oak.

"The valley is the wall. I only have to close the door."

They came down the eastern ridge in the dark, quietly at first, and then not quietly at all. Four hundred men, perhaps more, in black-smeared jackets and straw sandals, with spears and woodcutters' axes and a few swords, and at their head a big man on a shaggy pony with a long iron club across his saddle. They came down the slope and into the meadow, and then they saw the watch fires and the line of carts, and someone shouted, and they broke into a run.

"Now," said Ji Shan, quite softly.

The Garrison stood up.

Eight hundred spear points came over the top of the cart wall at once, in two rows, the front row low and the back row high, as Qi Jiguang had drilled every man in Wangyue to stand. The Black Charcoal ran into them in the firelight with nowhere else to go. The men at the front tried to stop and were pushed onto the spears by the men behind, and for a long ugly moment the meadow in front of the carts was a press of shouting men who could not go forward and could not go back.

Ye Xing shot the man on the pony through the shoulder. He dropped his club and swayed in the saddle, and another of her arrows took the pony's bridle and cut it, and the pony, which did not want to be there any more than anyone else, turned and bolted back up the meadow with its rider clinging to its neck.

Then Ye Chuan came out of the woods on the right.

He came at a gallop with a hundred riders behind him, along the foot of the western ridge and straight across the back of the Black Charcoal, and Mo Lin's two hundred spearmen came out of the oaks behind him at a run, shouting. The bandits looked over their shoulders and saw horses where the dark had been, and spears between them and the ridge, and the spears of the cart wall in front of them.

A man with an axe came over the carts near Ye Feng, scrambling up the upturned bed of a cart with his teeth bared. Ye Feng met him at the top. It was very quick. The axe came down, and Moonripple went across under it, and the man fell back the way he had come.

[Souls: 58.]

A second man came over behind him with a spear. Ye Feng turned the point aside with the flat of his blade, stepped in the way Indera had taught him, and took him across the chest.

[Souls: 59.]

Then it was over, almost as quickly as it had started. The Black Charcoal threw down their weapons in the firelight in a long ragged clatter, and knelt, because there was nothing else to do, and the Garrison came over the carts and stood over them with spears lowered, and Ye Chuan's riders walked their horses in a slow ring around the whole meadow.

Ye Chuan rode up to the cart wall and leaned down from his saddle, grinning, with his sabre still in his hand.

"Brother," he said. "I didn't even have to use the sabre. I just shouted."

"You shouted very well," said Ye Xing.

"Thank you, Sister. I've been practising."

The big man on the pony was found at dawn in the woods on the eastern ridge, where the pony had thrown him, with Ye Xing's arrow still in his shoulder. Lu Qing's clerks counted the rest in the morning light: thirty-one dead, a hundred and eighty-six kneeling, and the others fled back over the ridge into the hills. Two of the Garrison had died at the carts, and eleven were hurt.

[Kunyu held. The Black Charcoal is broken. Merit +400.]

[Those who laid down their arms may stay and work the land: 131 have chosen Kunyu.]

The charcoal burners came down out of the hills at noon.

They came in ones and twos at first, and then in families, thin brown people with their children on their hips, standing at the edge of the oak woods and looking at the valley. They looked at the silver ring in the grass, and the knoll with its banner, and the kneeling bandits being given bread by the river under the eyes of the Garrison.

Lu Qing went up to meet them himself, with two carts of bread and his tally board.

Ye Feng watched from the knoll as the quartermaster stopped in front of the first family and bowed, and said something, and handed the woman a round loaf. She stared at it. Then she broke it in half and gave the larger half to the child on her hip, and the child began, very seriously, to eat.

"Half the iron," said Teja, beside him, in a voice of deep disgust. "They took half the charcoal from those people, and now they wanted half the iron. And nobody fed them."

"Somebody will now."

Ji Shan was already at the line of stakes with a hundred of the Garrison and fifty of the kneeling bandits, marking out the first course of stones with a cord. He did not look up when Ye Feng rode down to say goodbye. Then, when Ye Feng had turned Qinglei for the road, he looked up after all.

"My lord," he called. "Before the first frost."

Ye Feng lifted a hand, and rode east toward home, with the bulls lowing behind him in the long grass of the Kunyu hills.

title: Chapter 78: Wangyue Commerce
content:
The yellow headcloths burned in a pit on the flat ground below the Barracks Halls, on a clear windy morning with the gulls crying over the harbour.

There were fifteen hundred of them. They had come to Wangyue in the spring on their knees, at the Town wall on the night of the wild and in the burned fields outside Huang, and for a season they had worked: on the wall, on Teja's road, on the salt pans and the docks and the new terraces of rice below the ridge. Wang Meng's law said that a man who knelt worked one season for the town that spared him. After that he was free to go, or to stay as a farmer, or to ask for a spear.

The season was over. Two thousand had finished it. Fifteen hundred had asked for a spear.

They stood now in long ranks beside the pit, in plain brown, with their headcloths in their hands. Hou Cheng stood in front of them. Behind Ye Feng, on the steps of the first Barracks Hall, stood Han Xin and General Qi and Ye Tian, and a crowd from the Commons had gathered along the edge of the flat ground to watch.

Hou Cheng did not make a speech. He had told Ye Feng the night before that he did not know how.

He took a folded yellow cloth out of his own coat. It was faded almost white, and torn along one edge, and Ye Feng had never seen it before.

"I wore one of these," Hou Cheng said to the ranks, in his rough loud voice. "Four years ago, in Ji province. I wore it because the man next to me wore one, and because I was hungry, and because the magistrate had taken my father's ox."

He looked at the cloth in his hand.

"Then I took it off and ran, and I came here, and the lord gave me a wall to hold instead of a village to burn. I have kept this in my coat every day since. I don't know why."

He dropped it in the pit.

For a moment nobody moved. Then a man in the front rank stepped forward and dropped his own headcloth in after it, and then the man beside him, and then the whole front rank. Then they were all coming forward together, fifteen hundred men filing past the pit and dropping the yellow cloths onto the fire, and the smoke went up thick and pale over the flat ground and blew away out to sea.

Wang Meng's clerks met them on the other side with bundles of new jackets. They were Wangyue purple, the same as every soldier in the town, and on the left breast of every one, stitched in pale thread, was a single ear of grain.

[WANGYUE 2ND INFANTRY: founded. 1,500 men. Commander: Hou Cheng.]

[The old Wangyue Infantry is now the WANGYUE 1ST INFANTRY.]

"The grain," said Ye Feng quietly to Han Xin, watching the first men pull on their jackets. "Whose idea was that?"

"Lady Pei's," said Han Xin. "She said that most of them took up the yellow cloth because they were hungry. She said that if they wear grain over their hearts, they will remember who fed them."

Ye Tian, beside them, said nothing, but when Hou Cheng came back up the steps with his face working, the big man put one hand on his shoulder and kept it there for a moment.

"A wall to hold," said Ye Tian. "You said it well."

"I didn't say it at all, Lord Ye Tian. I just dropped the thing in the fire."

"That was the saying."

The armour came out of the storehouses that morning, where it had waited since the defence nights: four hundred coats of fish-scale won on the Town walls, three hundred Han coats from Ren Que's camp, and five hundred cane shields still marked with the yellow column's paint. Hou Cheng had them scraped and oiled and handed out by height, and by the middle of the morning the 2nd Infantry looked like an army instead of a crowd of farmers holding spears.

The thirty silver-mane hides from the first defence night went the same day to the Commons saddlers, to be cut into saddle cloths for the officers of the Xingmu Guard, grey and shining, so that anyone on a battlefield could see where the lord's own guard was riding.

The weekly report came in the middle of the morning, while the new 2nd Infantry was still drawing spears from the armoury and arguing about who would stand in the front rank.

[WEEKLY REPORT · WANGYUE]

[People: 85,721. Refugees this week: 3,140, most from the Beihai roads. Talents among them: a boat-builder, two herbalists, a drum-maker.]

[Horses: 1,840. Foals: 14. Forge: spearheads 600, arrowheads 4,000, Nanyang sabres 300 (levies). UNMOVING WALL armour: first 40 sets (Heaven's Shields). HORN BOW WORKS: first 12 bows drying.]

[Herd Book: Livestock Den 1,579 head. Iron-Horns: 450 at home, 450 on the Kunyu range.]

[Kunyu: wall begun. Gull Isles: salt terraces working. Granaries: Suria has moved the rice.]

"Most from the Beihai roads," said Han Xin, reading over his shoulder.

"The Yellow Turbans in the west are moving."

"Toward Beihai," said Han Xin. "Toward Kong Rong."

He said the name the way he said the names of places on a map he had already studied.

"If they are, my lord, we will hear of it soon."

The ships came in on the afternoon tide, three of them, round-bellied northern traders with brown sails, coming in through the reef gap with the care of captains who had never seen it before.

Ye Feng was on the Harbour wall when they came in, with Ye Wan'er and Mi Zhu. He knew at once what they carried, because the wind was blowing off the sea and he could smell them. Horses. A great many horses, packed below decks after a long voyage.

"From the north," said Mi Zhu, shading his eyes. "Those are Zhongshan sails. Hebei." He went very still. "My lord, I think I know whose ships those are."

The first ship came alongside the quay, and her captain called down, and the harbour master called back and pointed at the board of fees. There was a pause while the captain read it. Then a short laugh from the deck, and two men came down the gangplank together.

They were very different. One was stout and cheerful, perhaps fifty, in a quilted coat too warm for the season, with a merchant's purse at his belt and a broad weathered face that looked as though it had spent most of its life in the wind. The other was thin and younger, perhaps forty, with a narrow clever face and quick dark eyes, and he was looking at the free port mark on the harbour steps the way Ye Wan'er looked at a price.

Mi Zhu went down to meet them, and the stout man threw his arms open.

"Mi Zhu! Mi Zhu of Donghai! They said you'd gone south and sworn yourself to a lord of the islands, and I said, never, not Mi Zhu, he'd never swear to anybody..."

"I did, Old Zhang," said Mi Zhu, embracing him. "I did. Come and meet him."

[Zhang Shiping. Talent: Horse Trader (B).]

[★★★ · Path: The Long Road North. He knows every horse fair from the Wall to the sea.]

[Su Shuang. Talent: Hard Bargain (B).]

[★★★ · Path: The Second Price. He never pays the first one.]

Ye Feng knew the names before the panels finished opening. Zhang Shiping and Su Shuang, great merchants of Zhongshan, who traded horses at Zhuo commandery. In the library book they had come to Zhuo in the year of the Yellow Turbans, met a young man selling straw sandals, admired him, and given him gold and iron and horses to raise his first troop. The young man's name had been Liu Bei.

He thought of Guan Yu, who was standing guard at the gate of the Mansion at that moment with his long blade, and of Mi Zhu, who was hugging Zhang Shiping on the quay. That's three.

"My lord," said Zhang Shiping, bowing so low that his quilted coat creaked. "We heard of your free port in Donglai, at the last harbour before this one. Everyone on the coast has heard of it. We had three hundred horses that we meant to sell in Xu, and we said, why go to Xu when there's a free port two days closer?"

"Three hundred," said Su Shuang. "Northern horses. Hill-bred, five years old, sound in the wind. We'll take three gold a head, my lord, which is a gift at a time like this, with the whole of Qingzhou wanting horses."

Ye Wan'er, standing beside Ye Feng, said in a small clear voice, "One and a half."

Su Shuang turned and looked at her, and his quick dark eyes went over her braid and her abacus and her pointed ears.

"Little sister," he said kindly, "you've never bought a horse in your life."

"No," said Ye Wan'er. "But I can smell your ships. You have been at sea a long time, and you had bad weather off Langya, because your sails are mended. Some of your horses are already sick. If you sail on to Xu, a third of them will be dead before you get there." She smiled at him. "One and a half, for the two hundred who are sound. And we will take the sick ones to our horse healer for nothing, and you can buy them back when they are well."

There was a long silence on the quay. Zhang Shiping looked at Su Shuang. Su Shuang looked at Ye Wan'er. Then, slowly, he began to laugh.

"Two," he said.

"Two," said Ye Wan'er, "and you stay in Wangyue."

They stayed.

By the evening Mi Zhu had them in the Harbour office with the door shut and a jar of Kahu's best rice wine on the table, and Ye Feng sat at the end of the table and listened to them plan.

"Horses for hire on the coast road," said Zhang Shiping, counting on his fingers. "Post horses between Wangyue and Kunyu, between Wangyue and Huang. Horses for sale to farmers and merchants and any lord who has the gold. A stable on the free port quay where every captain who lands can buy a horse to ride inland."

"Never the army's horses," said Ye Feng.

"Never, my lord," said Zhang Shiping at once. "Master Mi told us. The army's horses are the army's. We bring our own, from the north, and sell those."

"Hu Ba runs the army's herd," said Mi Zhu. "He will help you. He knows every horse in Wangyue by name."

"Then we'll call it the Moon Road Stables," said Su Shuang, "because the road from the north to the sea now ends at a moon."

Mi Zhu turned to Ye Feng then, and laid a sheet of paper on the table in front of him. It was covered in his neat merchant's hand.

"My lord," he said. "The trading house we spoke of."

Ye Feng read it. WANGYUE COMMERCE, it said at the top, and under it, in a list: The Mi Trading House on the Quay. The Crescent Wok House, eating houses and inns, under Kahu. The Half Moon Smithy, tools and ironware, never blades, under Tie Shou. The Green Lamp Clinic, salves and remedies, under Lady Maelis. The Moon Road Stables, under Master Zhang and Master Su, with Hu Ba. All goods to be sold under the name of Wangyue.

"Under Master Wang," said Ye Feng.

"Yes," said Mi Zhu. "With me to run it."

Ye Feng took up the brush and signed it.

[WANGYUE COMMERCE: founded. Chair: Mi Zhu, under Wang Meng. Branches: 5.]

Ye Wan'er, who had been sitting quietly at the other end of the table, looked up from her slate.

"Master Mi," she said, "Xingmu Commerce will buy all your sick horses' feed from the Green Lamp Clinic, at full price, because I promised. You should write that down before you forget it."

"I never forget a sale, Lady Ye."

"Then you won't mind writing it down," said Ye Wan'er.

It was dark when Ye Feng walked back up to the Mansion, and the yard was not quiet.

Ye Chuan was running round it as fast as he could go, laughing and shouting at the same time, with Ye Shuang a few paces behind him with her spear reversed, holding it by the blade so that the heavy butt end swung. Ye Tian sat on the Mansion steps with his arms folded and watched them, and Ye Xing sat beside him, and Ye Feng saw that Ye Xing was laughing so hard that she had to lean against her brother's shoulder.

"Who told her?" said Ye Feng.

"Lira," said Ye Xing, wiping her eyes. "She came back from Kunyu with the herders this afternoon. She said she promised."

"Brother!"

Ye Chuan shouted, going past for the third time.

"Brother, help me! I was eleven! It was a very small frog!"

"It was a toad," said Ye Shuang, and swung, and missed him by a hand's width.

Ye Tian, who never smiled, did not smile now either. But he moved his feet, slowly and without looking, so that when Ye Chuan came round the corner of the steps again, there was a big boot in exactly the right place.

title: Chapter 79: Three Hundred from Bing
content:
Fang Lei had been a mason for thirty-four years, and in all that time he had never worked on a wall he liked as much as this one.

It was not a beautiful wall. Walls were not meant to be beautiful. It ran along the top of the ridge above Wangyue from the sea cliffs to the hills, grey stone below and rammed earth above, with four square towers and a walk along the top wide enough for three men abreast. In one place, near the middle, it had broken. On the night of the wild something big had come against it in the dark, and the stones had gone, and men had died in the gap, fourteen of them, holding it until morning.

Fang Lei had arrived the next dawn, out of the mist under the great tree, with nothing but his trowel in his belt and his name in his mouth, and the lord had looked at him for a long moment in the way the lord looked at people, and then said, Can you mend it?

I can make it better than it was, Fang Lei had said.

That had been most of a month ago. Now the gap was nearly closed. He and Awang and their forty men had taken the broken stretch down to the living rock, every stone, and were building it back up the way a wall should be built, the big stones at the bottom bedded in lime and gravel, the face stones cut to fit so close that a knife would not go between them. Awang was a good mason, better than he knew, and argued about every stone. Fang Lei liked that too.

He was on the scaffold on the outer face of the wall, in the middle of the morning, when the boy on the tower shouted.

"Men on the west road! Armed men!"

Fang Lei put down his trowel and looked.

They were coming along the coast road from the west, where it came round the shoulder of the hills from the Huang country, in a long column, three abreast.

He counted them without meaning to, the way a mason counts courses. Three hundred, near enough. They were on foot, and they were ragged, in jackets so patched and faded that he could not tell what colour they had been, with bare legs and straw sandals and packs on their backs. Some of them were limping. One was being carried on a door between two others.

And yet.

Fang Lei had seen a great many soldiers in his life, in the bad years before the mist. He had seen magistrates' soldiers and bandits pretending to be soldiers and soldiers pretending to be bandits, and he knew how a column of beaten men walked, all strung out and staring at their feet. These men were not strung out. Every rank was three men exactly. The gaps between the ranks were exactly the same. And on every man's back, over the patched jacket, was a long shield, and every shield was clean, not new but clean, and oiled. The spear points over their shoulders caught the sun all together, every one of them bright.

The column stopped well outside bowshot from the wall, all at once, as though a single man had stopped. Nobody had shouted an order. Fang Lei had been watching, and he had not heard one.

Then one man walked out of the front of it, alone, and came up the road toward the gate.

He was not big. He was perhaps forty, of middle height and spare, in a coat of old lamellar armour so worn that half the plates had been replaced with leather, with a plain sword at his hip and his helmet under his arm. His face was thin and brown and very still. He walked up to the gate, stopped exactly at the edge of the ditch, and looked up at the guards on the tower.

"I am Gao Shun," he said. His voice was not loud, but it carried. "A captain of the Bing garrison at Yanmen, once. My men and I have walked from the north. We do not want to come in. We want to buy grain."

The sergeant on the tower called down to ask what he would pay with.

"We have no money," said the man called Gao Shun. "We have hands. We will work for it."

Awang went to fetch the lord, because nobody else thought of it, and Fang Lei went down the scaffold and out through the half-built gap in the wall to have a closer look, because he was fifty-one and could do what he liked.

The captain was standing where he had stopped, beside the ditch, with his helmet under his arm. He had not moved. Fang Lei walked up to him and stood beside him and looked at the gap in the wall from the outside, the way the captain was looking at it.

"You're building it on the rock," said Gao Shun after a while, without turning his head.

"All the way down."

"Good." A pause. "Most people don't."

"Most people are fools."

The captain turned his head then and looked at him, and Fang Lei saw that he was younger than he had first thought, and very tired, and that there were old scars across the backs of both his hands.

"Your lord," said Gao Shun. "Does he pay his soldiers?"

"Every month," said Fang Lei. "On the day. Master Wang counts it out himself."

"Does he feed them?"

"Better than he feeds himself. The lord eats at the Commons tables some nights, with whoever's there. I've seen him."

Gao Shun was silent for a moment.

"And when his soldiers go into a village," he said, "what do they take?"

Fang Lei thought about it, because it was a real question and deserved a real answer.

"What they're given," he said. "There's a law, Master Wang's law. A soldier who takes anything he's not given pays it back twice over, and gets the cane in front of the whole Barracks, and if he does it again he's out of the army, and out of Wangyue."

He shrugged.

"I've only seen it happen once. A spearman took a chicken from a fisherman's wife at Huang. They caned him on the flat ground in front of five thousand men, and the fisherman's wife cried, and the lord paid her for two chickens himself, because the spearman only had the money for one."

The captain looked at him for a long time without saying anything. Then he looked back at the wall.

"We will carry stone," he said, "if your master mason will have us."

"You'll carry stone whether I have you or not," said Fang Lei. "I've seen your shields."

The lord came down from the Mansion in the middle of the afternoon, on foot, with Han Xin and the big quiet Lord Ye Tian and the lady general Ye Shuang.

By then the three hundred were working.

Fang Lei had expected them to be useless. Soldiers were useless with stone, in his experience: they dropped it, and cracked it, and set it crooked and called it straight. These men were not useless. They came in a long line from the stone heap to the gap and passed the stones from hand to hand, the big ones on poles between two men, and never once dropped one. When Awang shouted for lime, the lime was there. When he shouted for a wedge, a man was already holding one out. They did not talk, and they did not stop. Every hour, without anyone telling them, a third of them sat down in the shade and drank water and ate a handful of rice, and then got up and took the place of another third, so that the work never slowed.

Their captain worked with them. He carried stone like everyone else.

Fang Lei saw the lord stop at the edge of the work and watch. He saw the lord's face change, the way it had changed on the morning Fang Lei came out of the mist, as though he were reading something written in the air over Gao Shun's head that nobody else could see. It was a strange look. It went on for a long time. Then the lord breathed out, slowly, and said something very quietly to Han Xin, and Han Xin nodded.

The lady general, Ye Shuang, was watching the three hundred too, with her arms folded and her spear in the crook of her elbow, and after a while she said, loud enough for Fang Lei to hear, "Look at their feet."

"What about their feet?" said the lord.

"They stand like spearmen even when they're carrying stone. Every one of them. Left foot forward." She tilted her head. "Somebody drilled those men for years, Brother. Somebody very hard."

The lord walked up to the stone line. Gao Shun saw him coming and set down the stone he was carrying, and straightened, and bowed, the short deep bow of a soldier.

"Captain," said the lord. "You're welcome in Wangyue. Come inside. Your men can eat at the Commons tonight, and sleep in the Barracks."

"Thank you, my lord," said Gao Shun. "We will eat what we have earned, at the end of the day. We will sleep outside the wall."

The lord looked at him.

"Why outside?"

"Because we are armed men you do not know," said Gao Shun, "and a lord should not let armed men he does not know sleep inside his walls." He paused. "And because I do not know you yet, my lord."

Fang Lei, on the scaffold, held his breath. He had seen lords strike men for less.

The lord only nodded.

"That's fair," he said. "Stay as long as you like. Eat whatever you earn. Watch whatever you want to watch."

He turned to go, and then turned back.

"And Captain. The man on the door. The one your men carried in."

Gao Shun's still face moved, very slightly.

"He has a fever. From a wound in his leg. We have no physician."

"We have a clinic," said the lord. "Lady Maelis. She's Eldari, and she's the best healer I've ever seen. If you'll let her, she'll come out to your camp. You don't have to come in."

For a long moment Gao Shun did not answer. Then he bowed again, lower this time.

"I would be grateful, my lord."

The healer came out at sunset, a slim pale woman with silver-grey eyes and a basket on her arm, with two Eldari girls behind her carrying water and linen, and went straight to the man on the door without looking at anyone else.
