Fang Lei stayed late on the wall that night, though there was no light left to work by. He sat on the half-built top of the gap with his legs over the outer face and ate his supper there, and watched the camp of the three hundred down by the road. They had made it in the dark, quickly, without fuss, a neat square of small fires with their shields stacked in rows and a guard at each corner. Even their cooking fires were in lines.

Awang came up beside him with a bowl of soup and sat down.

"I asked one of them what they're called," said Awang. "The young one with the bad tooth. He said they don't have a name. He said the captain says a name is something you earn, and they haven't earned one yet." He blew on his soup. "And I asked if they wanted some of Kahu's rice wine, because the Crescent Wok sent a jar up for the workers, and he said no. He said the captain doesn't allow it. Not a drop. Not ever."

"Never?"

"That's what he said."

Fang Lei thought about the oiled shields, and the ranks of exactly three, and the man who had carried stone all afternoon and then refused to sleep inside a wall he had helped to build.

"Well," he said, "he can have a wall without wine. I'll build him one."

Down in the camp, in the middle of the square, a single figure was still standing beside the man on the door, with the Eldari healer kneeling at his feet. Fang Lei could not see his face in the firelight. But he knew who it was, because nobody else in that camp would still have been standing.

title: Chapter 80: No Wine
content:
The Eyes had shown Ye Feng the captain's panel on the first afternoon, while Gao Shun was still carrying stone, and he had stood at the edge of the work for a long time reading it.

[Gao Shun. Talent: Breaker of Lines (B).]

[★★★★ · Path: The Seven Hundred. Every line he leads against is broken.]

He knew the name. He had known it before the panel finished opening, from the thick library book with the cracked spine, the one he had read three times in the school holidays. Gao Shun. His origins are not recorded. He had served Lü Bu, the greatest warrior of the age, and commanded a company of about seven hundred men that the histories called the Trap Breakers, because no trap and no line could hold them. Their armour and weapons were always fine and well kept. Every attack they made broke the enemy.

He had been upright and quiet, the book said. He did not drink. He took no gifts. He warned Lü Bu again and again, and Lü Bu did not listen. In peacetime Lü Bu took his seven hundred away and gave them to a kinsman, and in wartime gave them back, and Gao Shun never once complained. At the end, at Xiapi, when everything had fallen, he had gone to his death beside the master who had never trusted him, and said nothing at all.

He hasn't met Lü Bu yet, Ye Feng had thought, watching him set down a stone. He's walked right past him.

Han Xin had seen it in his face. "My lord knows this man," he had said, very quietly.

"I know what he'll be. If someone gives him the chance."

"Then my lord should be careful," Han Xin had said, "not to give it to him too quickly. A man like that does not want to be chosen. He wants to choose."

So for two days Ye Feng gave Gao Shun nothing at all except the wall, and the grain he earned, and a healer for his sick man.

The three hundred carried stone from dawn to dusk. At night they slept in their neat square of fires outside the wall. Maelis went out every evening with her basket, and before long the man on the door sat up and asked for rice. Gao Shun watched everything. Ye Feng saw him on the wall walk at sunrise, looking down into the town. He saw him at the edge of the flat ground at noon, standing perfectly still while Bayu drilled the new 2nd Infantry, watching the way the drill sergeants corrected the men without striking them. He saw him outside the Commons at supper time, looking at the long tables where soldiers and fishermen and farmers ate side by side, and at the back where the lord himself sat with a bowl of Kahu's fish soup between Ye Tian and a boy from the salt pans.

Gao Shun never came in. He only watched.

Koa came over from the Gull Isles one morning while the stone was still being carried, and brought a broad brown Nacari with him, a quiet man with sea-cracked hands and a long fishing spear, who stood at the back of the hall while Koa talked.

"The salt terraces need guarding, my lord," said Koa. "And the spring. Lady Wang's crossbow women are good, but they are only twenty, and the Brothers Pan know where we are now. Master Wang has given me five hundred of the Garrison. I need a man to lead them who knows the islands."

He turned and nodded at the man at the back of the hall.

[Hemi. Nacari. Talent: Reef Guard (B).]

[★★★ · Path: The Shallow Water. Every reef is his wall.]

"Hemi was born on the reef," said Koa. "He has fished every rock of the Gull Isles since he could walk. He knows where a boat can land and where it will tear its bottom out. If anyone comes at the islands, he will know where they will come before they do."

Hemi bowed without a word. Ye Feng liked him at once.

"Then he leads them," he said. "And Hemi, the spring on the big island has Lady Wang's name now. Nobody touches it."

"Nobody, my lord," said Hemi. It was the only thing he said all morning.

That evening, ten days after the Red Dunes, with the last of the wounded back on their feet, Ye Feng took the Family Army through the black door again.

[TOWER RECORD · STAGE 5 · THE SALT MOON MARSH · one month inside, one night outside]

[A Salt Queen flooded the pans of anyone who would not pay her. Ye Xing watched the tides for three days, then broke the Queen's own dykes on the turn of the water and took her barges at the last sluice.]

[Battles: 5. Fallen: 20, among them Mei Hua, a Daughter of the Sky, drowned saving a child. Wounded: 38.]

[Joined: about 5,000 followers with their families.]

[Rewards: silver 75,000, armour 1,500 sets, marsh horses 250, Merit +1,500. Tribute: 5,000 silver and salt every payday.]

[Kingdom special: SALT CRAFT. The Queen's pan masters can double a salt pan's yield.]

[Notable talent: Grandmother Ru, pan master. Talent: Brine Reader (B).]

[Talent group: the Dyke Breakers, eight sworn sluice men who fight with hooked poles. Talent: B.]

[Ye Family Army battle grade: TRAINED.]

In the morning, Gao Shun stood on the wall and watched five thousand strangers walk up the cliff path from the sea with salt rakes on their shoulders. He did not ask where they had come from, but Ye Feng saw him count them.

It happened on the road below the gate, on a bright cold morning.

A farmer from the Huang country came in with a cart of millet to sell in the Commons market, as farmers did every day now, and halfway along the road below the wall a soldier stopped him. The soldier was a big man, a veteran of the old Infantry from the first year, with a scar through one eyebrow and a good name in his company. He said something to the farmer, laughing, and took a sack of millet off the back of the cart, and slung it over his shoulder, and walked away up the road toward the Barracks. The farmer stood looking after him with his mouth open.

Thirty of Gao Shun's men were working on the road beside the gate when it happened. Gao Shun himself was among them, with a stone on his shoulder. He set the stone down and stood watching.

By the time Ye Feng came down from the Mansion, the whole road knew. The farmer was standing at the gate with his hat in his hands, explaining over and over to the sergeant that he had not wanted to make trouble, it was only one sack, the soldier had probably meant to pay. The soldier was standing on the flat ground below the Barracks with his captain beside him and the sack of millet at his feet, looking at the ground.

And all along the edge of the flat ground, without anyone calling them, men had gathered. The new 2nd Infantry, fifteen hundred of them, in their purple jackets with the grain ears on their hearts. Ye Feng saw their faces. He saw what they were thinking, because he would have thought it too. A veteran. One of the old ones. One of the lord's own. Now we'll see.

Beyond them, at the gate, Gao Shun stood with his arms folded, and did not move.

Ye Feng walked out onto the flat ground. Han Xin came with him, and Wang Meng, and Hou Cheng, whose face was dark.

"Is it true?" Ye Feng said to the soldier.

The big man did not lift his head.

"It's true, my lord. I thought... it was only one sack. I was going to pay him at the end of the month. I didn't think."

"You didn't ask him."

"No, my lord."

Ye Feng turned to Wang Meng.

"Master Wang. The law."

Wang Meng did not need to look anything up. He spoke in his dry clear voice, loud enough to carry to the edge of the flat ground and beyond it to the gate.

"A soldier who takes what he is not given pays it back twice over. He takes twenty strokes of the cane before the Barracks. A second time, he is put out of the army, and out of Wangyue."

"Twice over," said Ye Feng. "Two sacks of millet. From his wages, not from mine. And twenty strokes." He looked at the big man. "Today. Here."

The soldier's captain opened his mouth, and then shut it again.

They did it there, on the flat ground, in front of everyone. The big veteran took off his jacket and knelt, and the Barracks sergeant gave him twenty strokes, and the veteran did not make a sound. When it was over he stood up, slowly, and put on his jacket, and walked across the flat ground to the gate, where the farmer was standing, and gave him the sack he had taken and a string of coins for two more. The farmer did not know what to do with them. He held them as if they might burn him.

Then the veteran walked back and stood in front of Ye Feng, and waited.

"It's the first time," said Ye Feng. "So you stay. The cane is for what you did. The jacket is still yours." He paused. "Don't make me do it twice."

"No, my lord," said the big man hoarsely. "Never, my lord."

All along the edge of the flat ground, the men of the 2nd Infantry were very quiet. Then, slowly, they began to drift away, back to their drills and their tents and their meals, talking in low voices. Ye Feng did not need to hear what they said. He had seen their faces.

When he looked up at the gate, Gao Shun was gone.

He came at sunset.

He came alone, through the open gate, up the valley road and up the steps to the Mansion, in his worn armour with his helmet under his arm. He had never come through the gate before. The guards at the Mansion door looked at each other and let him pass, and he walked into the hall, where Ye Feng sat at supper with the Ye family and Han Xin, and knelt.

"I have served three masters, my lord," he said. "The first sold our grain to the Xianbei and let my men go hungry. The second let his soldiers burn a village because the headman was slow to bow. The third ran from the Yellow Turbans and left us on the wall at Yanmen to die, and we did not die, and so we walked south." He looked up. "Every one of them would have spared that soldier this morning. He was a veteran. He was their own. Nobody would have said anything."

"Somebody would have," said Ye Feng.

"Yes," said Gao Shun. "The farmer. To his wife. And to every other farmer on the Huang road, for the rest of his life." He bowed his head. "I have watched you for three days, my lord. If you will have my three hundred, they are yours. And so am I."

Ye Feng stood up and came round the table, and raised him himself.

"Your men told my mason that they don't have a name," he said. "That you said a name was something to be earned."

"They have not earned one yet, my lord."

"They carried stone for three days for a town that wasn't theirs, and never dropped one," said Ye Feng. "I think they've earned it."

[WANGYUE TRAP BREAKERS: founded. Commander: Gao Shun. Hard cap: 700. Answers to Han Xin.]

[Gao Shun's 300 sworn. The rest to be chosen from every branch.]

Gao Shun looked at the panel, which he could not see, in the place where Ye Feng was looking, and something moved in his still brown face.

"Trap Breakers," he said slowly. "That was what they called a company in the north once. Long ago. Before my time."

"It's yours now," said Ye Feng.

Han Xin was already laying a sheet of paper on the table. "Seven hundred, Captain," he said. "Never more. You will pick the other four hundred yourself, from every branch, the best men we have. Master Tie will give you the best armour the Wangyue forge can make. Indera, who teaches the lord the silat of his people, will be your deputy. She will teach your men to fight with their hands, close, when there is no room for a spear."

"Thank you, General."

At the end of the table, Ye Chuan, who had been listening with his chin in his hand, said suddenly, "Hou Cheng will want to drink to it."

As if he had been waiting for it, Hou Cheng came in through the door at that moment with a jar of Kahu's rice wine under one arm and two cups in his hand, grinning all over his rough face.

"Captain Gao," he said. "Welcome to Wangyue. My 2nd Infantry and your Trap Breakers will stand next to each other in every line from now on, so we should drink to it."

"I do not drink," said Gao Shun.

Hou Cheng's grin faded slightly.

"Not even tonight?"

"Not tonight. Not any night. Not my men either."

Gao Shun looked at the jar with no expression at all.

"A man who drinks before a battle is slow. A man who drinks after a battle talks. A man who drinks at all, sooner or later, does both."

There was a pause. Ye Shuang put her hand over her mouth. Ye Xing looked at the ceiling.

Then Hou Cheng sighed, very heavily, and poured both cups, and drank one, and then the other.

"Then I will have to drink yours, Captain," he said, wiping his mouth. "Every time. For the rest of our lives. It is the least a friend can do."

For the first time since he had walked up the coast road, Gao Shun smiled. It was a very small smile, and it was gone almost at once. But Ye Feng saw it, and so did everyone else at the table.

The rider came out of the dark an hour after midnight, on the west road, so fast that the guards on the gate tower had barely time to shout before he was at the ditch.

He pulled his horse up so hard that it reared, and sat it there in the torchlight, a long-boned young man with a long bow across his back and a quiver of black-fletched arrows at his hip, and his face grey with dust and exhaustion. The horse was blowing and shaking under him.

"Open the gate!" he called up. "I have a letter for Count Ye Feng! From the Chancellor of Beihai!"

Ye Feng had come down to the gate by then, woken by the guards' shouting, with Ye Shuang behind him with a lamp. He looked down from the tower into the torchlight, and the rider looked up, and Ye Feng knew him.

The last time he had seen that face, it had been lying in the ash beside him on a burning knoll outside Huang, with three black-fletched arrows laid on the ground in front of it.

"Taishi Ci," he said.

title: Chapter 81: The Letter from Beihai
content:
They brought him up to the hall of the Mansion with the lamps still being lit, and he would not sit down.

Taishi Ci stood in the middle of the floor in his dusty riding clothes with the long bow on his back, swaying very slightly, as if the floor were still moving under him the way his horse had. Lady Pei came in with a bowl of hot soup and put it into his hands, and he looked at it as though he had forgotten what soup was for. Then he drank it all in one long swallow, and gave her back the bowl, and bowed to her, and turned to Ye Feng.

"My lord," he said. "I promised you on the knoll that when you called me, I would come. I am sorry. This time it is I who must call you."

He took a letter from inside his coat. It was folded small and sealed with red wax, and the wax had cracked, and there was a dark stain along one edge that might have been water and might not.

Ye Feng broke the seal and read it standing.

The hand was elegant, the hand of a scholar, the characters small and perfectly formed even though the brush had clearly been moving fast. To the Count of Wangyue, from Kong Wenju, Chancellor of Beihai. The Yellow Turbans of Qingzhou, under their general Guan Hai, have surrounded the city with a host I cannot count. They have burned every village between the river and the hills. The granaries will last perhaps twenty days. I have four thousand men on the walls and ten times that many people behind them. I have asked for help from the provincial governor and had no answer. I ask you now, though I have no right to ask, and nothing to offer you but my gratitude, which I am told is worth very little.

There was more, but that was the heart of it.

He passed the letter to Han Xin, who read it in silence, and then to Wang Meng.

"How did you get out?" said Ye Feng.

Taishi Ci looked at the floor, and for a moment Ye Feng thought he was not going to answer. Then he said, quite simply, "My mother sent me."

He told it sitting down at last, at the long table, with a second bowl of soup in front of him that he did not touch.

When Ye Feng had left Huang, Taishi Ci had stayed with his mother, as he had said he would, until the harvest was in and she was strong enough to be left. Then word had come from the west. The Yellow Turbans were moving on Beihai, and the Chancellor, Kong Rong, was shut up inside with them all around.

"My mother told me to go," said Taishi Ci. "While I was away in Luoyang, in the trouble with the province, the Chancellor sent her food and gifts every month, though he had never met me. He did it because he had heard that I was a dutiful son. She said that a kindness like that is a debt, and a debt has to be paid, and that she would rather lose her son than have a son who did not pay his debts." He paused. "She is a hard woman, my mother. I love her very much."

So he had ridden to Beihai, alone, and found it surrounded, and waited for night, and gone through the Yellow Turban lines on foot with his bow and come to the wall and been let in.

"The Chancellor wanted to send to the governor again. I said the governor would not come. He asked who else there was." Taishi Ci looked up at Ye Feng. "I said there was a lord on the Donglai coast who had helped Huang when nobody else would, and who did not let his soldiers take so much as a chicken. The Chancellor said he had heard of you. He said he would write."

"And then you had to get out."

"Then I had to get out."

Something that was almost a smile touched the corner of Taishi Ci's mouth.

"There is a trick I had read about, in an old book. In the morning I rode out of the gate with two horsemen behind me carrying archery targets. The Yellow Turbans all stood up and took their weapons and watched. I rode to the edge of the ditch, set up the targets, shot at them until I had used all my arrows, and rode back in again. The next morning I did it again, and only some of them stood up to watch. After that, nobody stood up at all. They were cooking their breakfast." He shrugged. "Then one morning I rode out with the targets, and kept riding, through their lines and away, before they could find their spears. A few of them followed. I shot the ones who came close."

There was a short silence in the hall.

Ye Chuan, at the end of the table, said in a voice of deep admiration, "I'm going to steal that."

"You will have to wait until someone besieges you, Lord Ye Chuan," said Taishi Ci gravely.

"I'm patient. I can wait."

"He can't," said Ye Shuang.

Ye Feng was not listening. He was thinking of the library book, and a page he had read a long time ago in another world. When Guan Hai besieged Kong Rong at Beihai, Taishi Ci came to his aid. He broke out through the besiegers and went to Liu Bei at Pingyuan, who sent three thousand men, and the bandits scattered.

It had not said Wangyue.

"My lord," said Han Xin quietly beside him. "We should call the council."

They met at first light, every one of them, as they always did when something mattered.

Han Xin and General Qi sat on his right, and Wang Meng and Kirana on his left. The Ye family sat along one side, Ye Tian and Ye Xing and Ye Shuang and Ye Chuan, and at the end of their bench Ye Wan'er with her abacus. Guan Yu sat at the foot of the table with his long beard on his chest. Behind the benches stood the captains: Zhao Mu, Bayu, Saeli, Hou Cheng, and Gao Shun, who had been in Wangyue for four days and stood very straight at the back with his helmet under his arm. Taishi Ci stood beside him. Lady Wang sat beside her husband.

Wang Meng spoke first, because it was the end of the month and he would not let a council pass without the accounts.

[WANGYUE · MONTH'S END]

[Income: salt 410g · Wangyue Commerce and the Mi House 640g · livestock goods 240g · free port fees 90g · fish and boats 230g · tribute of the 11 villages 190g · Gull Isles salt 180g.]

[Wages and upkeep: 1,420g. (The Ye Family Army is paid by Xingmu Commerce.)]

[Treasury after wages: 1,950g.]

"For the first time since the founding," said Wang Meng, "the town earns more than it spends, and has some left over."

He looked down the table at Ye Wan'er, and inclined his head to her very slightly.

"Thanks in part to Lady Ye, who has taken the Family Army off my books."

Ye Wan'er turned faintly pink and pretended to count something on her abacus.

Then Ye Feng told them about the letter.

When he had finished, nobody spoke for a moment. Then Han Xin unrolled a map across the table, and they leaned over it.

"Beihai is three days' march to the west," said Han Xin. "Two, if we push. Guan Hai has perhaps eighteen thousand men around the walls, if General Taishi's count is right, and many more camp followers. Most of them are farmers with spears. Some are not. His own band are hill men who have fought for two years and are good." He touched the map. "They have been sitting around the city for a month. They are tired and bored and hungry, and they think nobody is coming."

"Six thousand," said General Qi. "We can send six thousand and still hold the coast."

"Which six thousand?"

They spent the next hour on it. In the end it was the Xingmu Guard, all of it, with Ye Shuang. Then the Wind Riders with Ye Chuan and the Mo brothers, and five hundred of the Daughters of the Sky with Ye Xing. Ye Tian came too, and his hundred Heaven's Shields, because he would not hear of staying behind. Last came Zhao Mu with five hundred of the 1st Cavalry, the Wangyue 1st Infantry with two thousand spears, and Gao Shun's three hundred.

"And the 2nd Infantry," said Ye Feng.

There was a slight pause around the table. Hou Cheng, at the back, went very still.

"My lord," said Kirana carefully, "the 2nd Infantry knelt to us only this season. Fifteen hundred men who wore the yellow cloth. You would send them against the yellow cloth?"

"That's why I'd send them," said Ye Feng. He looked at Hou Cheng. "Half of Guan Hai's men are farmers who joined because they were hungry. When they see fifteen hundred men who wore the same cloth, standing in our line in purple, with grain on their hearts, what do they think?"

Han Xin was smiling very slightly.

"That there is somewhere else to go," he said.

Hou Cheng's rough face had gone dark red. He stepped forward from the back of the room and bowed so low that his forehead nearly touched the table.

"My lord," he said hoarsely. "We will not disappoint you."

"I know."

Kirana would hold home, with every army that stayed, and Wang Meng the Town, and General Qi the coast and the fleet. Guan Yu would ride with the column.

"One more thing," said Han Xin. "General Taishi must ride ahead. The Chancellor must know we are coming, and when, so that he can come out of the gate at the right moment. A signal. Three fire arrows over the north wall." He looked at Taishi Ci. "It means going back through Guan Hai's lines. Alone."

"I have done it once," said Taishi Ci. "I can do it again."

Ye Wan'er caught Ye Feng in the passage outside the hall when the council broke up, with her abacus under her arm and ink on two fingers.

"Brother," she said. "Six thousand men for six days, perhaps eight. Rice, salt, dried fish, fodder for two thousand horses. Master Mi has the carts. Lady Pei has the bread ovens. I have already told the Green Lamp to send every salve they have, and I have put the Xingmu salve in with it, and I am paying for all of it." She took a breath. "And I have sent a boy to buy every arrow in the Commons market before the price goes up."

"You think it will?"

"When six thousand soldiers march out of a town, the price of arrows goes up," said Ye Wan'er patiently. "Everyone knows that, Brother."

He looked at her for a moment. Then he put his hand on top of her head, the way Ye Tian sometimes did to him, and she went pink again and did not move away.

"Thank you, Wan'er."

"You can thank me when you come home," she said. "Bring everyone back."

The column marched west at dawn, winding up the valley road and over the ridge, under the long new wall where Fang Lei's masons had stopped work to watch it go.

Taishi Ci had gone an hour earlier, alone, on a fresh horse from the army's herd, with two quivers of arrows and the long bow across his back. Ye Feng had walked down to the gate to see him off. At the edge of the ditch Taishi Ci had turned in the saddle and looked back.

"My lord," he had said. "On the knoll, I said I would come when you called. I did not think the first time you called would be to help me keep a promise to someone else."

"A promise is a promise," Ye Feng had said.

Taishi Ci had looked at him for a long moment in the grey light. Then he had turned his horse and gone up the west road at a canter, and the dark had swallowed him before he reached the first bend.

Now the sun came up behind the column, throwing their shadows long in front of them down the road toward Beihai, and Ye Feng rode at the head of it with Guan Yu on one side and Ye Shuang on the other, and did not look back.

title: Chapter 82: The Road to Beihai
content:
The column went west along the coast road and then inland, over the low brown hills that divided Donglai from Beihai, through a country that grew emptier with every li.

At first there were still farms, with people in the fields who straightened up to watch the soldiers pass and then bent again to their work. By noon there were farms with nobody in them. By evening there were only black squares in the fields where farms had been, and the smell of old smoke, and once, at a crossroads, a row of graves so fresh that the earth was still dark.

Ye Feng rode at the head of the column and looked at all of it, and said nothing.

The Wangyue 1st Infantry marched behind the Xingmu Guard, two thousand spears in a long purple river, and at its head walked a man Ye Feng had seen many times on the drill ground without ever quite noticing. He was square and heavy, with a neck as thick as his head and a face like a closed door, and he marched with his spear on his shoulder and never once looked to either side. When the road narrowed at a ford and the column began to bunch, it was this man who stopped, and turned, and said one word in a voice like a falling log, and the whole of the 1st Infantry closed up and straightened out as if a hand had smoothed it.

Ye Feng looked at him.

[Niu Da. Talent: Iron Wall (B).]

[★★★★ · Path: The Line That Does Not Bend. Where he stands, the line stands.]

"Han Xin," he said quietly. "Who is that?"

"Niu Da, my lord. A farmer's son from the Huang road. He came with the dawn arrivals in the first year and has stood in the front rank of every fight since the wild."

Han Xin's face did not change, but there was something pleased in his voice.

"He does not talk. He has never asked for anything. The 1st Infantry has no general yet, so I command it, and when I am not there, the men look to him. I have been meaning to tell my lord."

"He leads it now," said Ye Feng. "Under you. Tell him tonight."

"He will say yes, my lord," said Han Xin. "And nothing else."

The panel opened at dawn, while they were striking camp in a dry valley halfway to Beihai, with the horses steaming in the cold and the cooks putting out the fires.

[LORD RANKING · FOURTH MONTH]

[1. Ye Feng, Wangyue (Donglai, Qing). Count.]

[2. Shen Yan, Qilin Tower (Youbeiping, You). Count.]

[3. Zhao Lei, Iron Crown (Chenliu, Yan). Count.]

[4. Aisyah, Langya (Langya, Xu). Viscount.]

[5. NorthWolf, Frost Ridge (Bing). Viscount.]

[The first lord of the month receives a Talent Summon Card (B+), 500 settlers, 100 horses, 500 gold, and the monthly title FIRST LORD.]

He read it standing beside Qinglei with one hand on the saddle. Zhao Lei had made Count. That was new. Shen Yan was second again, as he had been every month, and Ye Feng thought of the private message after the auction, and wondered how close the numbers behind the panel were.

Then a second panel opened under the first, with a red border.

[TERRITORY DEFENCE RANKING · THE TOWN NIGHT.]

[1. Wangyue. Ten waves held. Both territories held. No villager harmed.]

[2. Qilin Tower. 3. Langya.]

[Territories that fell on the Town night: 211. Their lords walk as adventurers.]

[GRAND REWARD: WATCHFIRE BEACONS (Epic). A beacon tower on every territory under your banner. When one is attacked, all of them burn.]

He did not wait. He never waited with things like that.

[Watchfire Beacons: used.]

Far away to the east, too far to see, three towers of grey stone rose at that moment. One stood on the headland above Wangyue harbour, one on the white cliff of the Gull Isles beside Mak Senah's new salt terraces, and one on the knoll at the bend of the river in Kunyu, where Lu Qing would be sitting at his tally board and would look up and see it there, and probably write it down.

A third panel opened beneath the beacons, edged in red-gold.

[FIRST ON THE TOWN NIGHT, SECOND REWARD: THE CHIYAN DEN (Legendary). The Red Nightmare herd. Steppe warhorse mares of the north, and one stallion of the Red Hare's blood.]

[Every seventh dawn the Den gives foals. They are war-ready in one season. They will carry every army under your banner.]

[Chiyan Den: used.]

In Kunyu, on the long grass past the goat range, a stone stable opened out of the hillside. Inside stood forty mares with thick necks, and one stallion the colour of a forge coal. Lira would be there by morning. Hu Ba would be there before her.

He used the card too, standing there in the cold with the column forming up around him.

[Talent Summon Card (B+): used. The answer comes with the next dawn, in Wangyue.]

"My lord," said Han Xin, who had read the panels over his shoulder in the way that only Han Xin and Ye Xing ever seemed able to. "Two hundred and eleven."

"I saw."

"Two hundred and eleven lords who are lords no longer," said Han Xin. "Because you became a Town before they were ready."

He said it without blame, simply as a fact.

"Some of them will not forgive it."

"I know."

Ye Chuan rode up then from the back of the column, where the Wind Riders were forming, with his sabre slapping at his hip and his face shining.

"Brother! First again! That's four times! Mo Shan says if you're first one more time he's going to have it carved on your saddle!"

"I said I would carve it on Ye Chuan's saddle," said Mo Shan, riding up behind him. "Because he is the one who keeps telling everyone."

The world chat had been full of it all morning. Ye Feng read it in the saddle as they rode.

[World] HappyHotpotFist_hh: wangyue first AGAIN

[World] StoneBridgeLiu: free port + first lord + defence first. some people get all the luck

[World] DrunkPipaPoet_qq: it's not luck. my guild went to trade at his port last week. the fees are so low we stopped there just because it was cheaper than not stopping

[World] AshFieldLord_Wen: 211 territories fell on the Town night. mine was one of them. I was going to be a Town in 20 days. thanks wangyue

[World] FrostRidge: Survival of the fittest. Build walls before you build a name.

[World] IronCrown: Count. Finally. Third place is not where I intend to stay.

[World] QilinTower: Count Ye Feng is marching west with six thousand men. Toward Beihai, I'm told. I wonder what he wants there.

[World] DrunkTigerBoat666: wait what's at beihai

[World] YellowSkyWatcher: the yellow turbans are. like 20k of them

Ye Feng closed it.

"Shen Yan has someone watching us," said Ye Xing, riding beside him. She had read it too.

"He's had someone watching us since the auction."

"Then he will know what happens at Beihai the same night it happens," said Ye Xing. "So will everyone."

"Good," said Ye Feng.

The 2nd Infantry sang on the march.

Ye Feng heard it first in the afternoon, rolling up the column from the back like a wave: a slow deep song in many voices, the kind of song farmers sing to keep time when they are cutting grain. He had heard songs like it in the Huang country. The tune was one the Yellow Turbans sang. He had heard it outside the walls of Huang on the night of the fires, rising from three thousand throats in the dark.

But the words were different.

He dropped back along the column to listen. Hou Cheng was marching at the head of his men with his spear on his shoulder and his rough face set, and behind him fifteen hundred men in purple were singing, and what they were singing was about a valley by the sea, and a tree with silver leaves, and bread.

"Who changed the words?" he asked Hou Cheng.

"They did, my lord," said Hou Cheng. "Last night, round the fires. I didn't tell them to." He was silent for a few steps. "They say that when Guan Hai's men hear it, they'll know the tune. And then they'll hear the words."

Behind them Gao Shun's three hundred marched in perfect silence, in ranks of exactly three, with their long oiled shields on their backs. Ye Feng glanced at the Trap Breakers' captain and saw that he was listening to the song too, with no expression at all. But his left foot was keeping time.

They came over the last ridge an hour before sunset, and saw Beihai.

The city stood on a wide flat plain beside a slow brown river, a long grey wall with towers at the corners and a gate in each side, and smoke rising from inside it in thin straight lines. Around it, as far as the eye could see in every direction, were the camps.

There were hundreds of them. Ragged rings of tents and brush shelters and carts, with cook fires smoking and men moving among them like ants, and yellow banners hanging limp in the windless evening. Between the camps the fields were trampled flat and bare. On the north side, facing the city's north gate, was a bigger camp than all the others, ringed by a palisade of sharpened stakes, with a great yellow banner on a pole in the middle of it.

"Guan Hai," said Han Xin, beside him.

Ye Feng was looking at the walls. There were men on them, very small and very few, standing at long intervals along the battlements. Too few. On the north wall, above the gate, a single banner still flew, and it was not yellow.

"Twenty days," he said quietly. "His letter said the grain would last twenty days. That was when Taishi Ci left."

"Then they are close to the end," said Han Xin. "Which means they will come out of the gate when the signal goes up, whatever it costs them."

He spread his map across Qinglei's saddle in the last of the light.

"The Xingmu Guard and the riders go round to the north in the dark, my lord, by the river," he said. "When the fire arrows go up, the Chancellor comes out of the north gate. Guan Hai turns to face him. Then the Guard and the riders hit Guan Hai's camp from behind, along the river, where the palisade is weakest." His finger moved. "The 1st Infantry comes straight down from this ridge onto the camps on the east side, in line, with Niu Da in front. The 2nd Infantry comes behind them, singing." He looked up. "And the Trap Breakers go for Guan Hai's palisade gate. If they can break it, the camp is open."

"They'll break it," said Ye Feng.

At the edge of the group, Gao Shun said nothing. But he bowed, very slightly.

"And if the fire arrows don't go up?" said Ye Shuang. "If Taishi Ci didn't get through?"

Nobody answered her for a moment. Then Ye Xing did.

"Then we do not wait for his arrows," she said. "Look at the river side of the palisade, Brother. It is reed and brushwood, and it has not rained for twenty days. After midnight the wind comes down off these hills and blows straight across it toward the gate."

She touched the map beside Han Xin's finger.

"Give me two hundred bows on the riverbank. If the fire arrows go up, we light the palisade as the Chancellor comes out, and the Guard rides in through the smoke. If they do not go up by the fourth watch, we light it anyway, and the city will know what our fire means."

Han Xin looked at the line of the palisade, then at the dark hills, then at her.

"I meant to cut it with axes," he said. "Fire is better. We do it your way."

They waited on the ridge in the dark, six and a half thousand men lying in the brown grass with their weapons beside them, while the moon came up over the hills behind them and turned the river to silver. The Xingmu Guard and the riders had gone, silently, down toward the river an hour ago. Down on the plain the cook fires of the camps burned low and red. Somewhere a dog barked, and stopped.

Ye Feng lay on his stomach at the crest of the ridge with Moonripple beside him, and watched the north wall, and waited.

Ye Tian lay on one side of him, a long dark shape in the grass with his round shield beside him, so still that he might have been a fallen tree. Guan Yu lay on the other, with the long blade across his forearms and his beard tucked inside his coat so that it would not catch the moonlight.

"Brother," said Ye Tian, very low, after a long time. "When we go down, stay behind the 1st Infantry until the line has met them. Then do what you like."

"You think I'll run in front."

"I think you will want to," said Ye Tian. "Because Taishi Ci is in that city, and you made him a promise on the knoll. So you will want to be the first through the gate." He paused. "So will I. That is why I am telling you, and not myself."

On Ye Feng's other side, Guan Yu made a small sound that might have been a laugh, and stroked his beard through his coat.

"Lord Ye Tian speaks well," he murmured. "For a man who speaks so seldom."

"I save it," said Ye Tian.

Midnight came, and went.

Then, above the north gate of Beihai, a single point of fire leaped up into the dark, high and bright, curving over against the stars. A second followed it. Then a third.

title: Chapter 83: The North Gate
content:
The 1st Infantry went down the ridge in the moonlight in a single long line, two thousand spears, and the only sound was the brush of their feet in the dry grass.

Niu Da walked in the middle of the front rank with his spear held low. He did not shout. He did not look round. He simply walked, and the line walked with him, and when a stretch of it began to drift ahead or fall behind, it found its way back to him as water finds its level. Ye Feng walked behind the second rank with Ye Tian at his shoulder and the hundred Heaven's Shields around them, as he had promised.

The first camp on the east side of the plain was a ring of brush shelters and dying fires, with men asleep on the ground around them wrapped in their cloaks. Somebody sat up as the line came out of the dark. He stared at the wall of spear points walking toward him in the moonlight, and opened his mouth, and the line was on him before the shout came out.

It was not a battle, at first. It was a rout before a battle had begun. The men in the outer camps had been sitting in the fields around Beihai for a month, eating what they could steal and waiting for the city to starve, and they had not thought for one moment that anyone would come. They scrambled out of their shelters half asleep and saw the line, and ran. Some of them grabbed spears and stood, and the line met them and went on. Most of them did not stand at all.

Then the song started.

It came from behind the 1st Infantry, from the dark slope of the ridge, slow and deep, fifteen hundred voices rising together in the old harvest tune that every man in those camps had sung a hundred times. Ye Feng saw it go through the running crowd like wind through grass. Men stopped. They turned and looked back at the ridge, at the dark mass of men coming down it in purple with their spears on their shoulders, singing their song.

And then they heard the words.

Hou Cheng's voice rose over the singing, rough and enormous, louder than Ye Feng had ever heard it.

"Put down your spears! I wore the yellow cloth! I was hungry too! There's bread in Wangyue! Put down your spears!"

A man near Ye Feng, a thin farmer with a bamboo spear and bare feet, stood frozen in the firelight of a burning shelter and stared up at the ridge. Then he dropped the spear. He sat down on the ground where he was and put his hands on his head. The man beside him did the same, and then a whole group of them, ten, twenty, fifty, sitting down in the trampled field among the burning camps with their hands on their heads, while the 1st Infantry walked past them and on into the dark.

The north gate of Beihai opened a little after the third fire arrow had burned out.

Ye Feng could not see it from the east side of the plain, but he heard it: a great groaning of timber, and then a roar from the walls, thin and ragged at that distance, the roar of four thousand starving men who had decided that they would rather die outside than inside. Over the roar, faint and high and clear, came the sound of a horn.

"The Chancellor is out," said Ye Tian beside him.

The whole plain turned toward the sound. In Guan Hai's great camp in front of the north gate, drums began to beat, and torches swirled, and a flood of men began to pour out through the palisade toward the gate to meet the sally.

Then the river side of Guan Hai's camp caught fire, where Ye Xing's archers lay on the bank, and the hill wind took the flames toward the gate.

It went up all at once along a whole stretch of the palisade, a long sheet of flame, and through the flame and the smoke, in the red light, came the Xingmu Guard. Ye Feng saw them from across the plain, a long dark wave of riders with the silver crescent on their surcoats catching the firelight, and at their head a small figure on a grey horse with a spear held level. Ye Shuang. Behind and beside them, wilder and louder, whooping like boys at a festival, came the Wind Riders, a thousand and more, with Ye Chuan in front and the Mo brothers on either side, and in the middle of them, slower and heavier and far more frightening, the hundred iron-clad riders with their lances down.

Guan Hai's men had poured out of the front of their camp to meet the Chancellor. Now the back of it was full of horses.

"Now," said Ye Feng.

He did not have to say it to anyone. Ahead of him in the dark, he heard Niu Da's single word like a falling log, and the 1st Infantry wheeled toward the north as one man and went forward at a run.

The Trap Breakers reached the palisade gate of Guan Hai's camp at the same moment as the 1st Infantry reached the palisade.

Ye Feng saw it happen. The gate was a heavy frame of logs lashed together, swung shut now against the attack from the east, with a mass of Guan Hai's own hill men behind it and spears through the gaps. Gao Shun's three hundred came at it in a close block, their long shields locked over their heads and in front of them like the scales of some great creature, so tight that the spears behind the gate only scraped and slid off them. At the front of the block, under the shields, men were working with axes. Ye Feng could hear them over everything else, a steady heavy rhythm, chop and chop and chop, as calm as men cutting wood in a yard.

Then a section of the gate fell inward, and the shields opened, and the Trap Breakers went through.

They did not shout. Even then, they did not shout. They went through the gap in their ranks of three, shields up and spears low, and the hill men in front of them broke and gave way. Ye Feng saw Gao Shun himself in the first rank, his worn armour red in the firelight, his plain sword going in short economical strokes, never more than he needed.

Ye Feng went through the gap after them with Ye Tian and the Heaven's Shields, the front rank of them in the black iron of the Unmoving Wall, walking through the burning palisade as if the fire were rain.

Inside, the camp was chaos. Tents were burning, horses were loose and screaming, men were running in every direction. A hill man with a hooked spear came at Ye Feng out of the smoke, and Ye Feng turned the hook aside with Moonripple, stepped in, and cut him down.

[Souls: 60.]

Another came behind him with an axe. Ye Tian's shield came across, enormous and dark, and the axe rang off it, and Ye Feng went under the man's arm and took him in the ribs.

[Souls: 61.]

They pushed on toward the centre of the camp, where the great yellow banner stood on its pole, and the fighting grew thicker and harder. Two more fell to Moonripple in the press around the banner, one of them a big man in a captain's iron cap who nearly had him with a sweeping cut that went past his face close enough for him to feel the wind.

[Souls: 62.]

[Souls: 63.]

[Level 17 → 18.]

Guan Hai was at the foot of the banner pole.

He was a huge man, as big as Ye Tian, in a coat of iron scales with a yellow cloth tied round his helmet, on a tall black horse. In his hands he held a long-handled axe with a blade like a half moon, and around him were perhaps a hundred of his best men, the hill fighters who had been with him from the beginning, holding a ring around their general with their backs to the banner. He was roaring at them in a voice like a bull's, rallying them, and they were rallying. Men were coming back to him out of the smoke.

Ye Feng had taken two steps toward him when Guan Yu rode past.

He had not seen where Guan Yu had come from. He was simply there, on his big chestnut horse, riding out of the smoke at a walk with the long blade held low at his side and his green coat dark in the firelight. He rode straight through the ring of Guan Hai's hill men, and they parted for him without quite knowing why, the way men step aside in a crowded street for someone who does not slow down.

Guan Hai saw him coming and spurred his black horse forward with a roar, and swung the half-moon axe in a great flat arc.

The long blade went out once.

Ye Feng did not see exactly what happened. He saw the axe come round, and the long blade rise to meet it, and a great clash of iron and a shower of sparks, and the axe fly up out of Guan Hai's hands, turning in the air, and fall somewhere in the burning tents. He saw Guan Hai sway in his saddle with a long red line across his shoulder where the iron scales had parted. Then four of Guan Hai's hill men threw themselves at Guan Yu's horse, all at once, with spears, and another two grabbed their general's bridle and dragged the black horse round, and the black horse was gone, plunging away through the smoke and the burning tents toward the river.

Guan Yu dealt with the four spearmen in four strokes. Then he sat his horse at the foot of the yellow banner and looked after the black horse, stroking his beard, with no expression at all.

"He will not get far," said Ye Tian.

A bow string sang somewhere above them, and an arrow went through the smoke toward the river. Ye Feng turned and saw Taishi Ci on the palisade, standing on a cart against the logs with his long bow, already drawing again. But the black horse had reached the water, and plunged in, and the dark and the smoke closed over it.

Taishi Ci lowered the bow.

"He was too far," he said. "I am sorry, my lord."

"It doesn't matter," said Ye Feng. He was looking at the yellow banner. "He's beaten. That's enough."

Guan Yu rode forward, and swung the long blade once, and the banner pole came down. The great yellow cloth fell across the burning tents and caught fire at one corner, and all around the camp, as the hill men saw it fall, the fighting stopped.

Ye Tian beat the flame out with the flat of his shield before it could spread, and cut a strip from the scorched edge with his knife. He folded it small and put it inside his coat without a word. Ye Feng saw him do it and said nothing either. The Ye Family Army's banner had been waiting for a piece of Beihai.

Dawn came up over the plain of Beihai grey and cold, and showed them what they had done.

The camps were burning or burned, from the river to the hills. Everywhere in the trampled fields sat Yellow Turbans in long rows with their hands on their heads, thousands upon thousands of them, guarded by the 1st Infantry and the 2nd, and by the Chancellor's men who had come out of the north gate and were now standing among them looking dazed and thin and hollow-eyed. The rest of Guan Hai's host had fled in the night, west and south into the hills. Wang Meng's clerks would count them later. For now, Ye Feng only looked.

[Beihai relieved. Guan Hai's host broken. Guan Hai has fled.]

[Merit +2,600.]

[Those who laid down their arms may follow the lord who spared them: 5,670 have chosen Wangyue.]

[Wangyue fallen: 27.]

Twenty-seven. He read the number twice. Then he closed the panel.

He was standing by the north gate with Han Xin when the shout went up from the walls, and he turned and looked where the men on the wall were pointing.

There was a column coming along the road from the west. It was perhaps three thousand strong, foot and horse, under green banners, and it was coming fast, as though it had marched all night. At its head rode three men. One was a young man on a white horse, slight and long-armed, in plain armour, with a gentle open face. One was a huge man with a bristling black beard and eyes like a tiger's, carrying a long spear with a wavy blade like a serpent. The third rode a little behind, and Ye Feng could not see his face.

The column stopped at the edge of the trampled field, in front of the burning camps and the rows of kneeling men, and the young man on the white horse sat looking at it all for a long time.

Then he looked past Ye Feng, at the man on the big chestnut horse who sat beside him with a long blade across his saddle and a long beard on his chest.

Ye Feng did not need the panel. He had known the young man the moment he saw him, in the way you know a face you have seen in a hundred pictures. But the panel opened anyway.

[Liu Bei. Lord of Pingyuan.]

Guan Yu looked back at him across the field, politely, the way he would look at any stranger, and inclined his head.

title: Chapter 84: Debts
content:
Kong Rong received them in the hall of his residence in the middle of the morning, and he was not at all what Ye Feng had expected.

He had expected an old man. The Chancellor of Beihai was perhaps thirty, thin as a reed after a month of siege, in a scholar's robe that hung loose on him, with a narrow clever face and very bright eyes. He came down from his seat to meet Ye Feng at the door of the hall, which a Chancellor did not do for a Count, and took both his hands.

"Count Ye," he said. "I wrote that my gratitude was worth very little. I see now that I was wrong. It is worth exactly one city, and I would like to know how to pay it."

The hall was full. Kong Rong's officials stood along the walls, grey-faced and hollow-cheeked, in robes that had been fine a month ago. Han Xin stood at Ye Feng's shoulder, and Guan Yu behind him, and Ye Tian and Ye Xing and Ye Shuang. Taishi Ci stood a little apart, by the door, in his dusty riding clothes with the long bow on his back. And at the other side of the hall, on a bench that someone had brought for him, sat the young man from the white horse with his two companions standing behind him.

"You don't owe me anything," said Ye Feng.

"I owe you everything," said Kong Rong. "That is a different thing from owing you nothing, though I grant they can feel the same."

He smiled, and something of the scholar's sharpness came back into his thin face.

"Fortunately, I am a Chancellor, and a Chancellor has one thing that costs him nothing and is worth a great deal. He can write to the throne."

He turned to a clerk, who handed him a scroll.

"I have written a memorial to the court," said Kong Rong. "It tells the Son of Heaven that when the Yellow Turbans of Qingzhou came against Beihai and the provincial governor did not answer, the Count of Wangyue came with six thousand men and broke them in a single night. It says he took the surrender of eight thousand and did not let his soldiers take so much as a sack of grain from the people of Beihai. I have asked that he be named Protector of the Donglai Coast, with the right to keep soldiers and build walls and hold the coast against bandits in the name of the throne." He rolled up the scroll. "The court is slow. But it will read it. Everyone in Luoyang reads what Kong Wenju writes, if only to find out whom he is being rude about this time."

[Chancellor Kong Rong of Beihai has written to the throne on your behalf. Renown +600.]

[The court in Luoyang will hear the name of Wangyue.]

The young man from the white horse rose from his bench when the Chancellor had finished, and came forward, and bowed to Ye Feng.

It was a good bow. Everything about him was good, Ye Feng thought: the open gentle face, the plain armour with no gold on it, the long arms that hung almost to his knees, the warm voice. He looked like a man you would trust with your purse, your horse and your sister. He had looked exactly like that in every picture Ye Feng had ever seen of him.

"Count Ye," he said. "I am Liu Xuande, of Zhuo, though I keep Pingyuan now. The Chancellor sent to me as well, and I marched as fast as I could. You were faster."

He smiled, without any trace of resentment that Ye Feng could see.

"I am glad. My men had marched all night, and I do not think they could have fought the way yours did."

"They'd have fought," said Ye Feng.

"Perhaps. But I would rather not have had to find out."

Liu Bei's eyes moved past him, to Guan Yu, and stayed there for a moment. Then he spoke to Guan Yu directly, courteously, as one man to another.

"General. I watched you take the banner this morning. I have never seen a blade like yours, or a man like the one holding it. May I ask your name?"

"Guan Yunchang," said Guan Yu. "Of Hedong. I serve the Count of Wangyue."

Liu Bei looked at him for a long moment. "Have we met, General? I feel as though we have."

Guan Yu considered him gravely, stroking his long beard.

"I do not believe so, my lord," he said. "I think I would remember."

Behind Liu Bei, the huge black-bearded man with the serpent spear made a low rumbling noise in his chest, like a bear that has been woken, and said something under his breath that Ye Feng did not catch. Liu Bei raised one hand slightly without turning round, and the big man fell silent.

"You have a fine general, Count Ye," said Liu Bei, and bowed again. "Several fine generals. I hope that one day we will fight on the same side again, and that next time I will be in time to be useful."

"I hope so too," said Ye Feng, and found, a little to his surprise, that he meant it.

He watched the green banners go back along the west road an hour later, under the bright noon sky, and thought about a library book in another world. Liu Bei of Zhuo, who would found a kingdom. In that book, the general with the long beard had ridden beside him for thirty years. The horse dealers of Zhongshan had paid for his first army. Mi Zhu had given him his sister and his fortune.

Now all of them were in Wangyue, and Liu Bei had looked at Guan Yu as though at a word he could not quite remember.

"My lord," said Han Xin quietly, beside him. "That is a dangerous man."

"I know."

"Not because he is cruel," said Han Xin. "Because he is not. Men will follow him anywhere, for nothing. That is the most dangerous kind."

Taishi Ci knelt in the Chancellor's hall that afternoon, in front of everyone.

He knelt first to Kong Rong.

"Chancellor," he said. "You fed my mother when I could not, though you had never met me. I have come to repay it. If my lord the Count had not come, I would have died on your wall, and it would have been paid that way. He came, so it is paid this way instead."

He bowed until his forehead touched the floor.

"My mother will be content."

Kong Rong rose from his seat and raised him with his own thin hands.

"It is more than paid," he said. "Go well, Taishi Ziyi. And give your mother my respects, and tell her that she has a son who keeps his word, which is more than most mothers in this province can say."

Then Taishi Ci turned, and knelt again, to Ye Feng.

"My lord," he said. "On the knoll outside Huang, I told you I would come when you called. My debt to the Chancellor is paid. There is nothing left between me and my promise."

He laid his long bow on the floor in front of him.

"I am yours."

Ye Feng looked at him for a long moment, at the young man who had lain in the ash beside him on the burning knoll with three black-fletched arrows on the ground.

[Taishi Ci. Han. Talent: Archer (A).]

[★★★★★ · Path: The Arrow That Keeps Its Word. Riders who follow him strike first and strike true.]

He picked up the bow himself and gave it back.

"The Wangyue Cavalry has no general," he said. "Zhao Mu has led the 1st, and Hu Ba the 3rd, and Han Xin has commanded them all, because there was nobody else. There's somebody now."

[TAISHI CI sworn. General of the Wangyue Cavalry.]

Across the hall, Zhao Mu, who had led the 1st Cavalry since the first year, let out a great breath and grinned all over his weathered face, and came forward and clapped Taishi Ci on the shoulder so hard that the archer staggered.

"General," said Zhao Mu. "Thank the heavens. Now Han Xin can stop shouting at me."

"I never shout," said Han Xin.

"Not with your voice, General," said Zhao Mu.

Ye Xing found the physician in the afternoon, in the old temple by the east gate where the Chancellor had put the sick and the starving during the siege.

She came to fetch Ye Feng, which she almost never did, and led him through the streets without explaining, and he followed her because she was Ye Xing and did not waste anybody's time.

The temple was full. People lay on straw mats on the floor in long rows, men and women and children, thin as sticks, with their eyes too big in their faces. Among them, kneeling beside a little girl with his sleeves rolled to the elbow, was a man of about forty with a long grey-streaked beard and a lean brown face, holding a cup to the girl's lips and talking to her in a low voice, so that she smiled.

Beside him on the floor stood one of the boxes of salve that Ye Wan'er had sent with the column. It was open, and half empty.

"He has been here since the siege began," said Ye Xing quietly. "He came into the city before the Yellow Turbans closed the roads, because he heard there was a fever in the south quarter. He has not left since. The Chancellor's people say he has not slept more than two hours in a night for a month." She paused. "When the column came in this morning, he found our healers and asked them what was in the green jars. Then he asked for all of them."

The man looked up as they came in, and set down the cup, and rose. He was not tall. He moved like a much younger man, loose and light, like a deer or a bird.

[Hua Tuo. Talent: Divine Physician (A).]

[★★★★★ · Path: The Five Animals. Where he goes, the sick get up.]

Ye Feng knew the name. Everyone in his old world knew that name, even people who had never opened a history book. Hua Tuo, the great physician of the end of Han, who travelled from place to place and would take no office. He made a powder that put men to sleep so that he could cut them open and mend them, and he taught the Five Animals, the tiger and the deer, the bear, the ape and the bird, so that people could keep their bodies strong. In the book, he had died in prison, because a warlord had wanted him for his own physician and he had refused.

"My lord," said Hua Tuo. He did not bow very deeply. He looked at Ye Feng with sharp, kind, tired eyes. "Your green salve. Who made it?"

"The leaves are from a tree in my town," said Ye Feng. "Lady Maelis makes the salve. She's Eldari."

"I would like to meet her," said Hua Tuo. "I have been a physician for twenty years. I have walked from Pei to Langya and from Langya to the Wall. I have never seen a salve that closes a wound in a day."

He looked down at the little girl on the mat, who was watching him.

"Your soldiers brought it this morning, and they gave it to the Chancellor's men, and to the people of the city, and to the Yellow Turbans who had knelt, all from the same box. I watched them. They did not look to see whose wound it was before they put it on."

"They don't," said Ye Feng.

"No," said Hua Tuo. "I saw that." He was quiet for a moment. "I do not serve lords, my lord. I have refused three. A physician who serves a lord is a physician who must choose whose life matters more, and I will not choose."

"I'm not asking you to serve me," said Ye Feng. "There's a clinic in Wangyue called the Green Lamp. Anyone can come. Soldiers, fishermen, prisoners, strangers off the boats. Lady Maelis runs it, and she has more patients than she can heal. If you came, you wouldn't serve anyone. You'd heal them."

Hua Tuo looked at him for a long time.

"And the salve," he said at last. "I could learn how it is made?"

"Lady Maelis would teach you. If you'd teach her what you know."

Hua Tuo almost smiled.

"When this child can walk," he said, "and the fever in the south quarter is done. Then I will come and see this Green Lamp of yours."

They marched home when the wounded could travel, slowly, with five thousand six hundred Yellow Turbans and their families walking behind the column toward a town they had never seen, and a half-moon axe wrapped in the 2nd Infantry's baggage, because Guan Yu had found it in the ashes of Guan Hai's camp and given it to Hou Cheng.

"For your hall," Guan Yu had said. "So that every man who joins you knows what he came from, and who he is now."

A runner from Wang Meng met them on the road, with a letter.

The card answered at dawn, Wang Meng wrote, in his small dry hand. A Malay woman named Lela, from the river country, with a voice that carries across a drill ground without seeming to be raised. Her panel reads Banner Voice. I have made her deputy of the Garrison in Lu Qing's old place, since nobody else could be heard over the 2nd Infantry's new barracks. Also, Lady Ye Wan'er has bought a ship. She says it was cheap. I have not yet been able to find out what she means to put in it.

Ye Feng read the last line twice, and laughed out loud on the road, and Ye Chuan rode up to ask what was funny, and would not believe him.

But it was Kong Rong's last words that he thought about, on the long road east, when the column was quiet.

The Chancellor had walked him to the gate himself. At the threshold, while the others were mounting, he had taken Ye Feng's sleeve and drawn him aside, and said in a low voice:

"Count Ye. I have done you a kindness, and I would like to do you another, which is to warn you about the first. When Luoyang hears your name, it will send someone. Someone with a title in one hand and a list in the other."

His bright eyes were very serious.

"Be careful what they offer you. And be more careful still about what they ask for in return."

title: Chapter 85: Twenty-Seven
content:
The column came home through the Throat in the middle of the morning, and Wangyue came out to meet it.

They had heard it was coming since the beacon on the headland flashed the signal at dawn, and by the time the first riders came down the valley road, the road was lined from the Throat Wall to the harbour. Fishermen stood on the walls of the drying racks. Children sat on their fathers' shoulders. The Daughters of the Sky who had stayed behind stood in a long row outside their camp with their bows on their backs, and when the Daughters of the Sky rode past them, they began to call out names, and the Daughters of the Sky called back, and nobody could hear a word.

Ye Feng rode at the front on Qinglei, with Han Xin on one side of him and Guan Yu on the other. He was very tired, and very glad, and he found that he did not know what to do with his face.

"Smile, Brother," said Ye Chuan, riding up behind him. "They came all this way."

"They live here."

"They came all the way from their houses," said Ye Chuan. "That's a long way, for some of them. Old Crab's knees are terrible."

Old Crab was on the harbour wall, as it turned out, with his crooked hands cupped round his mouth, shouting for his son, who was riding in the fourth company of the Xingmu Guard and pretending very hard not to hear him.

Behind the soldiers came the people from Beihai.

There were more than five thousand of them, men who had worn the yellow cloth until the night of the north gate, and had walked behind the column all the way from the west with their families following as fast as they could. They came down the valley road slowly, in a long dusty line, looking at everything. They looked at the stone houses and the drying racks and the great tree on its hill above the town, with its silver leaves turning in the wind, and at the harbour full of boats. Most of all, they looked at the people of Wangyue, who stood on both sides of the road and looked back at them, and did not throw anything, and did not shout anything, and after a while began to hand them water.

Hou Cheng walked at the head of them, in his purple jacket with the grain-ear badge, with Guan Hai's half-moon axe wrapped in sacking over his shoulder.

"Tell them where they're going," Ye Feng said to him, at the foot of the Mansion steps.

"I've told them, my lord. Twenty times. They don't believe me."

"Tell them again."

Hou Cheng turned round, and put two fingers in his mouth, and whistled so loud that the horses jumped.

"Listen!" he shouted. "You'll sleep in the longhouses on the north meadow tonight. There's a roof and a blanket for everyone. Tomorrow Master Wang will give you a job, and you'll work a season for it, and you'll be fed while you work. Nobody is going to hang you. Nobody is going to sell you. If anyone tells you different, send him to me."

There was a silence along the road.

Then, near the front, a thin man with a child on his back said, in a hoarse voice, "And after the season?"

"After the season," said Hou Cheng, "you're Wangyue."

Wang Meng read the names in the afternoon.

There were twenty-seven new stones on the ridge, cut by Awang's masons in the days while the column was on the road, because the runners had brought the names home ahead of the army. The whole of Wangyue climbed the valley to stand among the rows, as it had for the fourteen, and the people from Beihai climbed with them, because Hou Cheng had told them to, and because they had nowhere else to go.

Wang Meng read slowly, in his dry careful voice, with the name of each man's village and the name of his mother. After each one he stopped and waited, and somewhere in the crowd someone said, Here. Where no one answered, a Daughter answered, as before.

Then Wang Meng read the fourteenth name, a young spearman of the 1st Infantry who had come from a burned hamlet on the Huang road and had no family left alive, and before any of the Daughters could speak, a voice answered from the very back of the crowd.

Here.

It was a man from Beihai, Ye Feng saw. A big rough man with a scar through his eyebrow and the pale mark of a headcloth still on his forehead, standing among his own people with his fists clenched at his sides. He looked frightened by what he had done.

Nobody turned round to stare at him. Wang Meng only waited a moment, as he did after every name, and read the next.

After that, the people from Beihai answered too, here and there, for the men with no one. Never the same voice twice.

Ye Feng stood at the head of the rows between Ye Tian and Ye Xing and listened to every name, and thought about the night at the north gate. Twenty-seven men had died to open it. They had died for a city they had never seen, for a Chancellor they had never met, and the men who had killed some of them were standing on the ridge now, saying Here for them, because nobody else would.

He did not know whether that was right. He only knew that it was better than silence, and that the board in the hall of the children's home would have liked it.

When it was over, Ye Xing put her small hand on his arm for a moment, very lightly, the way she did when she thought he was thinking too hard.

"It is a good thing, Brother," she said. "It only feels strange."

Hou Cheng hung the axe in the 2nd Infantry's hall that evening.

The hall was new, a long timber building at the end of the barracks row with a beaten-earth floor and a single wide door, and it smelled of fresh sawdust and the onions somebody had been frying behind it. The fifteen hundred men of the 2nd Infantry stood packed inside it shoulder to shoulder, and more stood outside the door, and Ye Feng stood near the front with Ye Tian, because Hou Cheng had asked him to come and he had not been able to think of a reason to refuse.

Hou Cheng climbed onto a bench and hung the half-moon axe on two iron pegs on the end wall, with its long handle across and its broad blade turned down. Beneath it he hung Guan Hai's great yellow banner, with its burned corner, folded small so that only the edge of the yellow showed.

He climbed down and looked at it for a long moment.

"That's what we were," he said. He did not shout. In the packed hall it carried anyway. "Every one of us. We followed that banner because we were hungry and somebody told us the sky would change."

He turned round to face them.

"Some of you followed Guan Hai himself. I know who you are. I'm not going to say it out loud." He paused. "The new men from Beihai will come here when their season is done, and some of them will want a spear. When they come in through that door, the first thing they'll see is that axe. And they'll know two things. They'll know where we came from, and they'll know where we are now."

Nobody cheered. They did not have to. Somewhere near the back, someone started to hum the old harvest tune with the new words, and after a while the whole hall was humming it, very quietly, so as not to wake the children in the longhouses down the road.

Ye Tian, beside Ye Feng, said nothing at all, but his left boot was keeping time.

The weekly report came at supper.

[WEEKLY REPORT · WANGYUE]

[People: 117,991 with the Beihai joiners. Refugees this week: 2,700. Talents among them: a rope-maker, a bone-setter, a woman who keeps bees.]

[Horses: 2,590. Foals: 11. Forge: spearheads 700, arrowheads 5,000, crossbow bolts 2,000.]

[Herd Book: Livestock Den 2,004 head. Iron-Horns: 450 at home, 450 on the Kunyu range.]

[Kunyu: wall half built. Gull Isles: spring cistern finished. Granaries: full.]

He read it twice, the way he always did, and put it down, and found that there was someone waiting at the door of the hall.

She was a small, square Malay woman of perhaps thirty-five, in a plain brown jacket with the purple armband of the Garrison, with her hair tied up under a dark cloth and her hands clasped behind her back. She stood at the door as if she had stood at many doors and expected to be kept waiting at most of them.

"My lord," she said. "Lela. Master Wang said you would want to see me when you came home."

It was not a loud voice. It was not even a deep one. But it went through the hall like a bell through mist, and at the far end of the long table, where Ye Chuan and Mo Shan had been arguing about a horse, both of them stopped talking and turned round.

[Lela. Malay. Talent: Banner Voice (B).]

[★★★★ · Path: The Voice That Carries. When she speaks on a field, the field hears.]

"I'm glad you came," said Ye Feng, and meant it. "Master Wang says nobody else could be heard over the 2nd Infantry's barracks."

"That is true, my lord," said Lela, without smiling. "They sing a great deal. I have asked them to sing more quietly after the drum. Most nights now they do."

At the end of the table, Ye Chuan leaned towards Mo Shan and said, not quietly enough, "I like her."

"Lord Ye Chuan," said Lela, without turning her head, "the Wind Riders' horses are tied in the lane behind the Garrison's armoury again, and the armourers cannot get their carts out. Before the drum, please."

Ye Chuan stood up so fast that he knocked over his bowl.

Ye Wan'er came to the Mansion last of all, when the lamps were lit and the hall was nearly empty.

She came in quickly, with her pale braid over one shoulder and an abacus under her arm and her grey eyes very bright, and sat down at the table across from him without being asked, which was how he knew that she was pleased with herself.

"Welcome home, Brother," she said. "Did you eat? You didn't eat enough. Ye Shuang says you gave your rice to a boy from Beihai on the road."

"He was hungry."

"Everyone from Beihai was hungry. You can't feed five thousand people from your own bowl." She pushed a covered dish across the table to him. "Sweet bean soup. Eat it."

He ate it. She watched him, the way she watched a merchant counting coins, and waited until he was halfway through before she spoke again.

"I bought a ship," she said.

"Master Wang told me. He said you said it was cheap."

"It is the cheapest ship I have ever seen." She paused. "It is also full."

"Full of what?"

Ye Wan'er only smiled, the small closed smile she had learned from watching Mi Zhu sell cheese, and stood up, and took back the empty bowl.

"Come down to the quay tomorrow, Brother," she said. "At dusk. Bring everyone."

She went out with the bowl and the abacus, and left him sitting alone in the lamplight.

From the window he could see the harbour, and among the fishing boats and the three great ships and the red-sailed junk, a fat round-bellied coaster that he had never seen before, riding low in the water at the end of the new quay, with all its hatches shut.

title: Chapter 86: Lanterns
content:
The Family Army had come out of the black door at dawn that day, back from the Hollow Hills.

[TOWER RECORD · STAGE 6 · THE HOLLOW HILLS · one month inside, one night outside]

[A mountain king kept his people underground in his mines, and his forts had no doors above the ground. Ye Xing worked out where the old air shafts must come up among the rocks, Mo Lin went down them, and the Heaven's Shields fought him in tunnels a shield wide.]

[Battles: 6. Fallen: 25. Wounded: 55.]

[Joined: about 6,000 followers with their families.]

[Rewards: silver 90,000, armour 1,800 sets, hill ponies 300, Merit +1,800. Tribute: 6,000 silver and copper every payday.]

[Kingdom special: MINERS AND SAPPERS. Men who can tunnel under a wall or open a mountain.]

[Notable talent: Dun Shi, tunnel master. Talent: Stone Ear (B).]

[Talent group: the Deep Eight, sapper brothers who fight with short axes in the dark. Talent: B+.]

[Ye Family Army battle grade: TRAINED.]

That same dawn a rider came in from Kunyu. The Chiyan Den had given its first foals, thirty of them, and one more that Lira had not counted on: a colt the colour of a banked forge, already as tall at the shoulder as a yearling. Hu Ba had slept in the straw beside him all night.

"He looks at the other foals, my lord," the rider said, "the way Qinglei looks at ours."

So the lantern night was a homecoming too.

By dusk there were more people on the new quay than Ye Feng had ever seen there, because Ye Wan'er had said bring everyone, and in Wangyue a thing like that did not stay a secret for long.

The generals came, and their kin. Han Xin came with Lady Wen and their son Han Wei, who had his wooden sword in his belt. General Qi came with Lady Wang, and their boy Qi Zuoguo ran on ahead of them along the quay, whacking the mooring posts with a stick. Wang Meng came with a slate, because he went nowhere without one, and Mi Zhu came with his clerks, looking at the fat round-bellied coaster at the end of the quay with the expression of a merchant who has heard a rumour and does not like not knowing whether it is true.

Behind them came the fishermen, and the soldiers off duty, and half the town.

Ye Wan'er stood on the deck of her ship with her abacus under her arm, beside a thin old man in a patched blue robe who looked as though he had not slept in a month.

"Brother," she said, when Ye Feng came to the foot of the gangplank. "This is Master Tang Yu, of Langya. He makes lanterns."

The old man bowed very low.

"Made, my lord," he said. "I made lanterns."

"Show them," said Ye Wan'er.

Two of her clerks went to the hatches and lifted the covers back, and the crowd on the quay leaned forward to look.

The hold was full of lanterns. They were packed in tiers from the keel to the deck, folded flat and stacked in bundles tied with string, hundreds upon hundreds of them. There were round red lanterns and long white ones, lanterns shaped like rabbits and fish and lotus flowers, lanterns painted with cranes and plum trees and little boats on blue water. There were so many that the clerks could not see the bottom of the hold.

"Three thousand two hundred," said Ye Wan'er. "I counted."

Nobody said anything for a moment.

"Master Tang made them for the household of a great family in Langya," she went on, "for a festival this autumn. The steward ordered them in the spring and promised to pay when they were done. When they were done, the steward said the family no longer wanted them and would not pay. Master Tang had borrowed for the paper and the bamboo and the paint. His creditors took his workshop, and then his ship, and then they tried to sell the lanterns, and nobody wanted three thousand lanterns in summer." She shrugged. "So I bought the ship. The lanterns came with it, and so did his debts. I paid those too. They were less than the ship."

"Why?" said Mi Zhu, who could not help himself.

Ye Wan'er turned her grey eyes on him.

"Because Wangyue has a free port and no night market, Master Mi," she said. "And every free port in the world has a night market. Ships come in at dusk. Their crews have wages in their pockets and nowhere to spend them. Our people work all day and have nowhere to walk in the evening. So." She tapped the abacus. "We hang the lanterns along the quay. We rent the stalls by the night. The quay fees pay for the oil. Wangyue Commerce takes the rents. Xingmu sells tea."

She smiled at him sweetly.

"And Wangyue Commerce buys the lanterns from me. At a fair price."

Mi Zhu looked at the hold for a long moment, and then at Wang Meng, who was already writing on his slate.

"What is a fair price," said Mi Zhu slowly, "for three thousand lanterns that nobody in Langya wanted?"

"Then name a price," said Ye Wan'er, "for a night market that nobody in Langya has."

They haggled on the gangplank for the length of time it took the sun to touch the sea.

Ye Feng did not follow most of it. Nobody did, except Wang Meng, who wrote the numbers down as they went past and occasionally raised his eyebrows. Ye Wan'er asked for two silver a lantern. Mi Zhu offered three copper. Ye Wan'er reminded him that the Mi house had once sold cheese in Donghai at half its worth for a whole season. Mi Zhu said that was an old story and nobody remembered it. Ye Wan'er said that Lady Ye Wan'er remembered it, and so did Master Mi's own agent in Donghai, who had written to say so. Mi Zhu put his hand over his eyes.
