In the end they settled at sixty copper a lantern, and a tenth of the stall rents to Xingmu for the first year, and a stall at the head of the quay for Xingmu Leaf Tea, rent free, for as long as the market stood.

"You've been robbed, Master Mi," said General Qi, who had enjoyed every moment.

"I know, General," said Mi Zhu. "I have known it since the first number. I am only trying to decide how much."

"Nineteen gold and twenty silver," said Wang Meng, without looking up from his slate. "The rents will pay it back within the month."

Mi Zhu took his hand away from his eyes.

"Within the month?"

"If the ships come," said Wang Meng.

"They'll come," said Ye Wan'er. She looked at Ye Feng. "Brother? You haven't said anything."

"I'm thinking," said Ye Feng, "that we should hang them tonight."

They hung them that night.

The whole quay helped, and half the soldiers, and all the children. Ye Tian's Heaven's Shields stood on each other's shoulders to tie them to the masts of the boats along the quay. The Daughters strung them on ropes between the drying racks. Tang Yu went up and down the quay in his patched robe telling everyone how to fold them out without tearing the paper, almost in tears, because nobody had ever hung three thousand of his lanterns at once.

When the sun was gone and the first stars were out, Kahu came down the quay with a lit taper, and lit the first lantern, a great round red one at the head of the quay, under the Moon Banner. Then the children ran along the ropes with tapers of their own, and the lights went down the quay one after another, red and white and gold, until the whole harbour was a ribbon of light reflected in the black water.

Ye Feng stood at the head of the quay and watched it, and remembered something he had not thought about in a very long time.

At the children's home, when he was seven or eight, a temple in the town had sent them paper lanterns for the Mid-Autumn festival, one for every child. They were cheap red ones with a candle inside on a wire, and the children had carried them round the courtyard in a long line after dark, singing a song that most of them did not know the words to. His had caught fire almost at once. It had gone up in a single bright flash, and he had stood there holding the bare stick and trying very hard not to cry, because the older boys were watching.

One of the volunteers had knelt down beside him, a young woman whose name he had never learned, and given him her own lantern without a word, and walked the rest of the line in the dark.

He had forgotten her. He had not forgotten the lantern.

"Brother," said Ye Shuang, beside him. "Are you well?"

"I'm well," said Ye Feng. "I was thinking about a lantern."

Ye Shuang looked along the quay at three thousand of them.

"Which one?" she said.

The stalls went up before the lanterns were all lit, because Wangyue was not a town that waited for anything.

Kahu set up the Crescent Wok House at the head of the quay under the great red lantern, with two iron pans the size of shields and a line of hungry soldiers before the first pan was hot. Ye Wan'er's clerks set up the Xingmu tea stall beside it. Mak Senah brought salt in little bags with the moon stamped on them. The Mi house brought Wangyue Cheese and dried fish and pearl buttons. The fishermen's wives brought rice cakes wrapped in leaves. The crews of two merchant ships from Langya, who had come in on the afternoon tide, came ashore with their wages in their pockets and stood at the end of the quay with their mouths open.

Then the people from Beihai came.

They came down from the longhouses on the north meadow in a slow, wary crowd, because the lights had drawn them, with Hou Cheng walking in front of them in his purple jacket. They stopped at the edge of the quay, where the lanterns began, and did not come any further. Ye Feng saw the scarred man from the ridge among them, with a little girl holding his hand.

Kahu looked up from his pans and saw them standing there.

He did not say anything. He only filled a bowl with fried noodles and fish and gave it to the nearest of his helpers and pointed, and the boy carried it to the edge of the quay and gave it to the scarred man, and came back for another.

"Who pays for those?" said Mi Zhu, beside Ye Feng.

"I do," said Ye Feng. "Tonight."

"My lord cannot feed five thousand people from one wok."

"That's what my sister said," said Ye Feng. "About my rice bowl."

Mi Zhu sighed, and went and spoke to Wang Meng, and a few minutes later two of the Mi clerks were carrying a sack of rice down to Kahu. The fishermen's wives were handing rice cakes to the children at the edge of the quay, and after a while the people from Beihai came in among the lanterns, slowly, and walked along the quay looking at the lights like everyone else.

There was a race on the harbour wall before the night was out, because there always was.

Ye Chuan started it, as he always did. He said that the Wind Riders could carry a lit lantern from one end of the wall to the other faster than any Daughter of the Sky ever born, without the candle going out. Su Wan said that was the most foolish thing she had heard since the last foolish thing Ye Chuan had said. Then she picked six of her women, and Ye Chuan picked six of his riders, and the whole quay crowded onto the harbour wall to watch.

The Wind Riders ran so fast that every one of their lanterns went out before the halfway mark. The Daughters walked. They walked the whole length of the wall at a steady pace, with their lanterns held perfectly still, and arrived at the far end with six candles burning while Ye Chuan and his riders were still trying to relight theirs from a fisherman's pipe.

The quay roared.

"Lord Ye Chuan owes the Daughters a pot of sweet bean soup," said Lela, from somewhere in the crowd, in a voice that carried to the far side of the harbour, and everyone who had not heard about the race already heard about it then.

At the foot of the wall, Ye Feng saw Ye Tian standing very still among the children with a white rabbit lantern in his great hand. A small girl from Beihai had given it to him to hold while she ate a rice cake, and he was holding it as carefully as he held his shield, with his serious face lit from below, waiting for her to finish.

He did not move until she came back for it.

The Langya captains found Lady Wang at the end of the evening, by the Xingmu stall, where she was drinking tea and watching her son try to eat a fish bigger than his head.

"Lady," said the older of the two, bowing. "They tell us the Qi Family Fleet sails these waters."

"It does," said Lady Wang.

"Our ships come up from Langya every ten days, for the free port. We have lost two cargoes to the Brothers Pan since the spring. If the fleet would sail with us, from Langya to here and back, we would pay."

Lady Wang put down her cup and considered him, a small sharp woman with a pink new scar on her forearm from the Town night, looking at a man twice her size as though he were a cargo she was pricing.

"How much is a cargo worth to you, Captain?"

"Two hundred gold, Lady. On a good run."

"Then the escort is ten gold a ship each way," said Lady Wang. "Paid at the quay, before we sail. If we lose your ship, you pay nothing. We have not lost one yet."

The captain opened his mouth, and looked at her scar, and at her husband standing behind her, and shut it again.

"Ten gold," he said. "Lady, you have a bargain."

"I know," said Lady Wang, and picked up her tea.

It was nearly midnight when Kirana found him.

She came along the quay through the thinning crowd in her plain dark coat, with the light of the lanterns sliding over her face, walking quickly, the way she walked only when something mattered. She did not stop at the stalls. She did not look at the lanterns.

"My lord," she said quietly, at his shoulder, so that no one else would hear. "Forgive me for the hour. Koa's boats are back from the north."

"And?"

Kirana looked out past the lanterns at the dark mouth of the harbour, where the reef gap opened onto the open sea.

"They have found the nest," she said.

title: Chapter 87: The North Meadow
content:
Fen woke in the longhouse before dawn because the roof was not leaking, and the quiet of it frightened her.

For a long moment she lay still on the straw mat under the new blanket, listening. Her daughter was breathing against her side. Her son was asleep across her feet, as he had slept every night since they left the village, so that nobody could take her away without stepping on him first. On her other side, her husband lay on his back with his eyes open, looking at the roof beams.

"It's dry," said Shu Ping quietly.

"I know."

"It rained in the night. I heard it."

Fen listened again. Outside, water was dripping from the eaves into a puddle, slowly, in the grey light. Inside, there was nothing. No drip on her face. No wet straw. No cold creeping up through the mat from the ground. There were three hundred people asleep in the longhouse around her, and the only sound was the breathing of three hundred people who were, for the first time in a year, not cold.

She had not cried at the north gate, when the yellow banner came down and the men in purple came through the smoke and she had thought they would all be killed. She had not cried on the long road east. She lay on her mat in the dry longhouse and cried now, very quietly, so as not to wake the children, and Shu Ping put his big rough hand over hers and did not say anything at all.

The clerks came at sunrise.

There were six of them, young men and women with slates under their arms and purple armbands, and they set up a long table at the end of the north meadow and called the people from the longhouses one family at a time. Fen had expected soldiers. There were no soldiers, except for two old men of the Garrison leaning on their spears by the gate, who looked as if they would rather have been fishing.

"Name?" said the clerk, when it was their turn. She was a Malay girl of perhaps seventeen, with ink on her fingers.

"Shu Ping," said Fen's husband. "Of Ziyang, west of Beihai. This is my wife, Fen. My son. My daughter."

"Your trade?"

Shu Ping was silent for a moment.

"I was a farmer," he said. "Then the magistrate took the land for a debt my father owed. Then I carried a spear for Guan Hai."

The clerk wrote something down. She did not look up, and her face did not change.

"A farmer," she said. "Good. Master Wang needs diggers for the new channel on the Kunyu road. You will be fed at noon and at sundown. Your season is ninety days. After the season, you may ask for land, or a trade, or a spear." She turned to Fen. "And you?"

"I can spin," said Fen. "And weave. And cook."

"The rope walk needs spinners. A rope-maker came with the refugees last week, and he has more hemp than hands." The girl wrote again. "The children go to Teacher Xu's school in the mornings. It's free. They get a rice cake at the door."

Fen stared at her.

"Free?"

"The lord pays for it," said the clerk, and for the first time she looked up, and smiled a little. "Everyone asks that. Next, please."

The rope walk was a long low shed by the harbour, open at both ends, with a smell of hemp and tar, and the rope-maker was a cheerful bald man from Yan province who talked from the moment Fen arrived until the moment she left. She did not mind. Her hands knew the work, and while her hands worked, she could look.

There was a great deal to look at.

From the end of the rope walk she could see the whole harbour, the boats and the three great ships with their tall masts, and the strange red-sailed junk, and the fat coaster where the lanterns had come from. The lanterns were still hanging along the quay, unlit now in the daylight, swinging a little in the wind off the sea. Beyond the harbour wall, the sea was very blue. On the headland above it, a stone tower stood with a fire basket on top, and a soldier in purple walked round it, round and round.

At noon, she took her son and daughter to the cookhouse at the head of the quay, because the rope-maker said that anyone working a season could eat there. They sat at the end of a long bench with their bowls of fish and rice and ate without speaking, the way people eat who are not sure the food will still be there if they stop.

Halfway through, her son stopped eating and pulled her sleeve.

"Mother," he whispered. "Look. It's him."

A young man had come into the cookhouse with a group of soldiers, tall and lean, with long black hair tied half up and a short neat beard, in a plain dark coat with a blue sash, and a sword at his side in a worn grey sheath. He looked tired. He was talking to the big general beside him, the one with the red face and the beard to his belt, and laughing at something.

The cook saw him and started to clear the best table by the window.

"Kahu," said the young man, quite gently, "no. There are people eating there."

He took his bowl and sat down at the end of the nearest bench, among his soldiers, three places away from Fen, and ate his noodles exactly like everyone else.

Fen did not dare look at him. She looked at her bowl. But she could not help hearing, and what she heard was the lord of Wangyue asking a young soldier with a burned hand how his mother was, and listening to the answer, all of it, which was long, while his noodles went cold.

When he got up to go, her daughter, who was five and afraid of nothing, said loudly, "Thank you for the noodles."

Fen's heart stopped.

The lord turned round. He looked at her daughter, and then at Fen, and she saw something in his face that she had not expected, a kind of surprise, as if nobody had ever thanked him for anything before.

"You're welcome," he said, very seriously. "They're Kahu's. He makes the best noodles on the coast."

Then he was gone, and the big cook was standing over their bench with a ladle, filling her daughter's bowl again.

In the afternoon her son came back from the school with a rice cake in one hand and a slate in the other. There were three characters on the slate that he had written himself, and he would not stop showing them to everyone in the rope walk, including the rope-maker, who said they were the finest characters he had seen since he left Yan, and gave him a piece of string.

"It says Wangyue," said her son proudly, pointing. "And this one says moon. Teacher Xu says the moon is the same moon over Beihai and over here."

"Teacher Xu is right," said Fen, and had to go and look at the sea for a while.

On the way back to the meadow in the evening she saw the yard below the barracks, where soldiers were practising. A young woman with her hair tied back tight was fighting a laughing man with a curved sabre, spear against sword, so fast that Fen could not follow it, while a crowd of soldiers shouted and bet copper on the result. The young woman knocked the sabre out of the man's hand. He fell over on purpose, on his back in the dust, with his arms spread wide like a dead man in a play.

"I yield," he said to the sky. "Sister, I yield. Tell Su Wan I'll make the soup tomorrow."

"You'll make it tonight," said the young woman, and walked away without looking back, and the soldiers roared.

"That's Lady Ye Shuang, the lord's sister," said a fisherwoman passing Fen on the path, as if Fen had asked. "And the one in the dust is Lord Ye Chuan, his brother. They do that every evening. It's better than a play."

Fen walked on. She thought about the camps outside Beihai, and Guan Hai's captains, who had laughed too, sometimes, in the evenings. They had never laughed like that.

Shu Ping came home after dark, with mud to his knees and blisters on both his hands, and sat down on the mat beside her and ate his supper, and for a long time said nothing.

"The channel is hard," said Fen at last.

"The channel is good," said Shu Ping. "We dug three hundred paces today. The foreman says it will water two villages." He turned his bowl in his hands. "Fen. On the ridge, the day we came. When they read the names."

"I know. I was there."

"There was a boy. From the Huang road. He had no mother to answer for him." Shu Ping's voice was very low. "I was at the north gate that night, on the other side of it. Maybe it was me. Maybe it was the man next to me. I don't know. I'll never know." He put the bowl down. "So I said Here. Because somebody had to, and it should have been one of us."

Fen took his blistered hand and held it.

"When the season is done," said Shu Ping, "I'm going to ask Hou Cheng for a spear. I want to stand in that hall, under that axe." He looked at her. "Unless you say no."

Fen thought about the dry roof, and the rice cake at the school door, and the lord of Wangyue sitting at the end of a bench letting his noodles go cold while a boy talked about his mother.

"I won't say no," she said. "But you'll finish the channel first."

Shu Ping laughed, for the first time since Ziyang, so loudly that half the longhouse woke up and shouted at him.

She woke again before dawn, because of the bells.

They were ships' bells, many of them, down in the harbour, and the sound of oars, and voices calling across the water in the grey light. Fen got up and went to the door of the longhouse, and found half the north meadow already standing outside in the wet grass, looking down at the sea.

The fleet was going out.

They came out through the reef gap one after another, the three great ships first with their tall red sails, then the junk, then a long line of smaller boats behind them with purple pennants at their mastheads, and the silver crescent on every pennant catching the first light. On the decks of the great ships, Fen could see soldiers standing in their ranks, in armour, with bows and spears, and horses' heads looking out over the rails.

"Where are they going?" someone said.

Hou Cheng was standing at the edge of the meadow with his arms folded, in his purple jacket.

"North," he said. "To the islands. To the Brothers Pan."

The name went through the crowd on the meadow like cold water.

Fen knew that name. Everyone from Beihai knew that name. In the spring, Guan Hai's host had taken a town on the coast and could not feed the people in it. A black ship had come into the bay at night, and Guan Hai's captains had sold two hundred of them, the old and the weak and the young women, for rice. The ship had flown a banner with two black hands holding a knife.

Fen's sister had been one of them.

She stood in the wet grass with her hand pressed hard over her mouth, and watched the red sails go north along the coast, smaller and smaller, until the sun came up out of the sea and she could not see them any more.
